Phosphate (PO43-)1.01 mmol/L0.70-1.40 mmol/l
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)42 mm/hour<10 mm/hour
C-Reactive Protein (CRP)6 mg/L<10 mg/L

A blood film shows a normocytic anaemia and some rouleaux formation. Urinalysis reveals 2+ of protein.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Multiple myeloma: The rapidly increasing severity of back pain that does not vary with time or movement is significant. Although her calcium is not elevated, her globulins are (by virtue of the fact her total protein is raised and albumin is relatively normal), as is her ESR. She also has renal impairment and multiple areas of vertebral collapse. Multiple myeloma is a disease in which there is accumulation of malignant plasma cells, generally derived from one clone in the bone marrow. It is characterised by the production of a monoclonal immunoglobulin that can be detected in the serum or urine. It is often associated with bone pain, kidney disease and anaemia. Diagnostic tests include bone marrow examination, the presence of more than 10% plasma cells being required for diagnosis. A skeletal survey is required for lytic lesions and serum/urine electrophoresis is needed to identify the presence of paraprotein. Urinalysis can be performed to identify Bence Jones protein. Treatment is based around melphalan chemotherapy. In patients under 65 years of age, bortezomib is often used as an induction therapy for those patients going on to high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation, which often leads to a prolonged remission compared to conventional chemotherapy.

B. Renal cell carcinoma: Renal cell carcinomas can metastasise to the lymph nodes, bone, liver, lung and brain, so it would be one of the differentials for this patient. Renal cell cancer can present with bony involvement, anaemia and renal impairment, However, the protein level would usually be normal to low and the overall picture of this patient with raised ESR coupled with vertebral collapse and renal impairment, is more in keeping with a diagnosis of myeloma. Renal cell cancer patients often present with haematuria, unilateral abdominal pain, abdominal mass, fatigue, anorexia and weight loss.

A. Osteoporosis: Patients often present with back pain and fractures (including compression fractures) worsening slowly over time. The key points to note are the raised protein levels, renal impairment, raised ESR and proteinuria, which are not in keeping with a diagnosis of osteoporosis, meaning that this is incorrect.

D. Osteoporosis and over-diuresis: Osteoporosis tends to have a more insidious onset. This patient's picture is also not in keeping with a patient who has been over-diuresed. If that were the case, you would expect the patient to have a low sodium and potassium alongside a raised urea and creatinine. However, this patient has normal electrolyte levels.

E. Squamous cell lung carcinoma: This diagnosis is a possibility in this patient. The X-ray commented on an enlarged heart border, but an X-ray is unable to exclude a central mass. The cancer could have spread to the bone but you would usually expect a raised calcium, either secondary to bony involvement or due to a paraneoplastic phenomenon of hypercalcaemia of malignancy in squamous cell lung cancer. This patient's clinical picture does not quite fit with this and, as such, means it is not the most likely diagnosis for this patient.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a 24 hour history of unilateral swelling of the left leg. She has recently flown back to this country from Australia. She is previously fit and well, does not smoke and is on no medication. She has no family history of note.

Other than the swollen leg, examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound of the deep veins of the leg confirms an above-knee deep vein thrombosis, and she is commenced on enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily subcutaneously and started on 10 mg of warfarin. On the second day after starting warfarin she has developed black lesions over her buttocks. Platelet count remains stable at 205 × 109/l.

What is the most likely cause of the lesions over her buttocks?
questions.explanation:
B. Protein C deficiency: This woman has developed warfarin-induced skin necrosis (WISN); this occurs when warfarin is started and there is a defect in the protein C anticoagulant pathway. Protein C is vitamin K dependent and falls rapidly following the commencement of warfarin, leading to an initial paradoxical prothrombotic state: this explains why heparin is started concurrently with warfarin, to cover this initial period. The condition has been reported in association with most forms of thrombophilia, but defects in the protein C pathway (classically protein C deficiency, but also including protein S and activated protein C resistance) are the most common pre-existing conditions. In WISN, microthrombi form in the blood vessels of the skin, particularly in adipose areas such as buttocks and breast. The condition is severe, and plastic surgery is often required. Treatment is supportive, with vitamin K and possibly fresh frozen plasma to replace protein C levels. Prostacyclin and protein C infusion have been trialled. Warfarin can be reintroduced at a lower loading dose, but recurrence may occur.

E. Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome: This occurs either in isolation or against a background of SLE and is associated with recurrent venous thrombosis and other features such as livedo reticularis.

A. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type 2: HIT is associated with the development of necrotic skin ulcers, although the maintenance of a stable platelet count counts against this as the underlying diagnosis.

C. Prothrombin gene 20210 mutation: The prothrombin gene 20210 mutation is a cause of thrombophilia, rather than a cause of protein C deficiency in association with warfarin initiation.

D. Antithrombin III deficiency: Antithrombin III deficiency is associated with recurrent thrombosis, and is seen as an autosomal dominant congenital disorder and in patients with severe proteinuria. It is not associated with commencement of warfarin.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of fatigue, shortness of breath and abdominal discomfort. She has a past medical history of sickle-cell disease, for which she regularly takes hydroxycarbamide 500 mg twice daily. Her temperature is 36.1°C, heart rate 100 bpm and BP 90/60 mmHg. Her respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and her oxygen saturation is 96% on air.

On examination, she appears lethargic. She is cool to the touch, with a capillary refill time of four seconds. Auscultation of her chest is clear, with vesicular breath sounds throughout both lungs. Her heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is distended and tender to palpation, particularly in the left upper quadrant.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)60 g/l120-160 g/l
White cell count (WCC)9.4 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)208 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Reticulocyte count3%0.5-2.5%

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
D. Sequestration crisis: The clinical presentation of sudden-onset fatigue, abdominal pain and shock in a young adult with sickle-cell disease is highly suggestive of a sequestration crisis. A sequestration crisis is characterised by the sudden pooling of blood in the spleen or liver, leading to rapid splenomegaly and hypovolaemic shock due to a sudden decrease in circulating blood volume. It most often presents in children but can also present in adults, albeit less frequently.

B. Aplastic crisis: An aplastic crisis is characterised by decreased erythropoiesis due to infection with parvovirus B19. This results in severe anaemia and a reduction in the reticulocyte count. In this case, the reticulocyte count is raised, which suggests that the bone marrow is trying to overcome the anaemia. Additionally, the presentation of an aplastic crisis does not typically include sudden-onset abdominal pain and hypovolaemic shock, as seen in a sequestration crisis.

A. Acute chest syndrome: Acute chest syndrome is a serious complication of sickle-cell disease, characterised by fever, chest pain and respiratory symptoms. Often, pulmonary infiltrates are seen on a CXR. Although abdominal pain can occur in acute chest syndrome due to splenic infarction, the presentation described here is more consistent with a sequestration crisis, given the signs of hypovolaemic shock and significantly low Hb levels.

C. Haemolytic crisis: A haemolytic crisis in sickle-cell disease is characterised by an increased rate of red blood cell destruction. leading to anaemia, jaundice and reticulocytosis. While abdominal pain can occur in a haemolytic crisis, the presentation described here is more suggestive of a sequestration crisis, particularly given the presence of hypovolaemic shock and rapid onset of symptoms.

E. Vaso-occlusive crisis: A vaso-occlusive crisis is the most common type of sickle-cell crisis and is characterised by significant pain due to microvascular occlusion by sickled red blood cells. Commonly affected areas include the upper and lower limbs. While abdominal pain can occur in vaso-occlusive crises, the sudden onset of symptoms, in combination with shock and a significant drop in Hb level, is more suggestive of a sequestration crisis.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a 1-week history of dark urine and severe fatigue. On further questioning, she admits to increasing tiredness over a matter of weeks. One day before admission, she developed severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. On examination, she has pallor, jaundice, an enlarged tender liver and ascites.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)79 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)3.2 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)89 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)101 fl76-98 fl
Peripheral smearMild polychromasia
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)144 IU/L10-40 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)130 IU/L5-30 IU/L
Bilirubin54 μmol/l2-17 μmol/l
Urine Haemosiderin++
UrobilinogenPositive

Abdominal ultrasound reveals an enlarged liver, ascites and absent flow in the hepatic veins.

What single test would you request to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
options: D. Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 expression
questions.explanation:
D. Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 expression: This patient has paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) complicated by acute hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome). PNH is an acquired clonal disorder of haematopoietic stem cells, characterised by a variable combination of intravascular haemolysis, thrombosis and bone marrow failure. A somatic mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan-A (PIG-A) gene on the X chromosome leads to deficiency of several glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI)-linked molecules. Deficiency of decay accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) and the membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis (MIRL, CD59) increases susceptibility to complement-mediated lysis of blood cells. Currently, diagnosis is made by flow cytometric evaluation of blood, which confirms the CD55 and CD59 deficiencies and deficiency of expression of other GPI-linked proteins. This test is replacing older, complement-based assays (such as Ham's test and the sucrose lysis test) because it is less affected by blood transfusion, is more sensitive and specific and it measures the size of the PNH clone, which is useful for follow-up.

A. Viral hepatitis serology: This patient does not have viral hepatitis. Although with similar presentation symptoms of fatigue, dark urine, abdominal pain and jaundice, there would not be a disturbance of flow across the hepatic veins or evidence of haemolysis or anaemia.

B. Liver biopsy: A liver biopsy would not be diagnostic for PNH. It may show evidence of scarring or fibrosis. There is a high risk of bleeding with liver biopsies and, with low platelets and altered liver chemistry, it may not be advisable.

C. Inherited thrombophilia screen: PNH is an acquired condition. It is not inherited and so would not give a diagnosis of PNH on testing for inherited thrombophilias. It is likely that a thrombophilia screen would be largely negative. One study has shown an increase in anti-phospholipid antibody in some patients with PNH, although it is unsure how this affects the patient.

E. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) assay: Looking for G6PD deficiency is not appropriate in this instance. G6PD deficiency does produce haemolysis and jaundice but it is an X-linked inherited condition unlike PNH, which is acquired and doesn't affect males and females differently.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of easy bruising and menorrhagia. On the day of presentation, she developed 'heaviness' in her left arm and slurred speech. She is taking tranexamic acid, prescribed for the menorrhagia. She has no previous medical history of note. According to her husband, she was incoherent and confused for half an hour but is now alert and orientated.

Examination shows a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15, normal neurological examination and normal speech. Her temperature is 37.5°C her heart rate 105 bpm and her blood pressure 130/70 mmHg. Her heart sounds are normal. She has several bruises on her shins and forearms. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain is normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)85 g/l135-175 g/l
Platelets (PLT)17 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)102 fl80-100 fl
Reticulocytes130 × 109/L25-85 × 109/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)735 u/l140-280 u/L
Blood filmLow counts, numerous schistocytes
Prothrombin time (PT)15 s11-14 s
Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT)33 s25-35 s
Pregnancy testNegative

Her tranexamic acid is stopped. She is treated with plasmapheresis and prednisolone.

Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term intervention following the acute episode?
questions.explanation:
C. Daily aspirin: The results show anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and lactate dehydrogenase level, implying haemolysis, and the presence of schistocytes is most compatible with a microangiopathic mechanism. Coupled with low platelets and fluctuating neurological signs, this is classical for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Treatment for this is urgent plasmapheresis with fresh frozen plasma or cryosupernatant, which is thought to significantly reduce mortality, although there is a lack of randomised controlled trials in this area. Steroids are usually given alongside plasmapheresis in the acute setting. In this patient, tranexamic acid is prothrombotic and may be worsening the condition, and hence it has been stopped.

The condition is caused by an acquired autoantibody to the metalloproteinase ADAMTS13, the function of which is to control the size of von Willebrand's factor multimers. As a result, ultra-large von Willebrand's factor multimers, with enhanced activity, accumulate and cause increased binding of platelets to small blood vessels. The platelets (PLT) count falls and red cells are damaged when they pass through the narrowed vessels, causing microangiopathy. Once the PLT count reaches around 50, patients are started on long-term aspirin to reduce the risk of platelet aggregation.

A. 3-monthly plasmapheresis: Plasmapheresis is indicated in the acute setting of thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Ideally, it should be started within 24 hours of presentation as a delay in treatment decreases the chance of response. Around 90% of patients will respond to plasma exchange within three weeks. There are a number of complications associated with plasma exchange, including infection, venous thrombosis, hypotension due to large fluid shifts and serum sickness. Furthermore, plasma exchange increases the likelihood of the development of red blood cell antibodies. Due to the high likelihood of recovery following initial treatment, and the risks associated with plasma exchange, regular plasmapheresis is not recommended.

B. 3- to 4-monthly platelet transfusion: Platelet transfusion has previously not been recommended in patients with TTP, as it was thought to trigger the worsening of the disease. However, a retrospective review does not support this. Platelet transfusion is most likely to be considered in the acute setting if a patient is bleeding or when invasive procedures are required for plasmapheresis, alongside the administration of folic acid (as there is presumed deficiency from haemolysis and high demand for folate). However, long-term platelet transfusion is not recommended as the platelets (PLT) count should recover with prompt plasma exchange treatment.

D. Daily cyclophosphamide: Cyclophosphamide and other immunosuppressants, including rituximab and ciclosporin, may be used as second-line agents after initial treatment with plasmapheresis and steroids. However, their use is often only supported by a small number of cases studies and therefore, specialists will guide these decisions.

E. Splenectomy: Splenectomy was used before the invention of plasma exchange and there is some retrospective evidence that showed a good response to treatment. However, splenectomy puts patients at higher risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria. It is currently recommended as a last option for intervention in the acute setting due to the relative safety and transient risks of plasmapheresis. It is not recommended as a long-term treatment.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old nurse presents to the ENT Department with a flu-like illness. She gives a 10-year history of tendency to have a blocked, stuffy nose and frequent recurrent coughs and colds. The Occupational Health team has also noticed that she failed to show a response to hepatitis B and tetanus vaccinations.

In which immunoglobulin is she likely to be deficient?
questions.explanation:
A. IgA: This patient is most likely to have IgA deficiency, which is particularly associated with recurrent sinus infections due to encapsulated bacteria such as Haemophilus influenzae. Selective IgA deficiency is probably the most common of the primary immunodeficiency disorders, but it may also be asymptomatic. In Caucasians, IgA deficiency is said to occur in 1 in 600-700 individuals. There is often a deficient response to polysaccharide-based vaccinations. In patients with IgA deficiency, 10-44% of patients may have anti-IgA antibodies; this risks a severe reaction to IgA-containing products such as blood, plasma or immunoglobulin.

B. IgE: There are few case reports in the literature regarding IgE deficiency.

C. IgD: IgD immunodeficiency is quite rare, and individuals with this condition do not seem to be predisposed to infections.

D. IgM: Sometimes, in cases of IgA deficiency, compensatory IgM increase may occur.

E. IgG: IgG immunodeficiency is also common. IgG-subclass deficiency and its importance have been characterised. Antibodies against pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens are predominantly IgG2 and, to a lesser degree, IgG4. Antibodies against protein antigens, such as tetanus, are predominantly IgG1 and, to a lesser degree, IgG3. Finally, antibodies against large extracellular parasites, such as Schistosoma and Filaria organisms, exclusively belong to the IgG4 subclass. The history of sinus infections in the present scenario points towards IgA immunodeficiency.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old woman is admitted with confusion. She has no past medical history of note and was previously fit and well. Examination reveals small petechial haemorrhages on the legs and pale conjunctivae. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly detectable. The chest is clear and thorough systemic examination reveals no abnormalities except for a fluctuant Glasgow Coma Scale.

Observations: heart rate 110 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, temperature 38.4°C and O2 sats 97% on room air.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)93 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)13 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)34 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)142 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)5.1 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)100 IU/L30-130 IU/L

Chest X-ray (CXR)Lung fields clear, no other abnormalities detected

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: C. Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome
questions.explanation:
B. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): TTP is classically associated with the pentad of clinical signs and findings: confusion, pyrexia, kidney disease, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. The patient in this case exhibits all of these criteria, although it should be noted that not all patients will display all five. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a condition that causes a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. The exact aetiology is unclear, but it has been found to be associated with auto-antibodies to ADAMTS13, a protein responsible for cleaving von Willebrand factor (VWF) into smaller units. Ultra-long VWF is very pro-thrombotic and can form a mesh in the vessels which causes fragmentation of red cells (a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia). It can be associated with pregnancy and the postpartum period, but is also seen in non-pregnant individuals. TTP is characterised by five symptoms or signs: confusion, pyrexia, kidney disease, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Patients are often treated with plasma exchange. Eculizumab may be useful in patients with refractory disease.

D. Chest sepsis: Sepsis can present very similarly to TTP, i.e. with a fever, confusion and signs of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (if deteriorated to disseminated intravascular coagulation) and is always a very important differential diagnosis to be considered in these patients. However, the history and examination suggest that there is no clear source of sepsis, the patient's CRP is not raised and the chest X-ray is normal.

A. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP): HSP classically affects children post-mild infection. This would be a differential diagnosis for petechial haemorrhages on the patient's legs, but this patient is suffering from many other symptoms (fever and confusion) which would not be explained by HSP. Furthermore, whilst HSP can cause deranged renal function, the low platelet count, raised bilirubin and signs of haemolysis on the blood film seen in this case are not associated with HSP.

C. Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome: HELLP syndrome is associated with confusion, haemolysis and low platelets, as seen in this case. However, it is only seen in the setting of pregnancy, or recent delivery, usually associated with pre-eclampsia.

E. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): SLE is the great mimic and can affect all organs including the kidneys, brain and blood. However, SLE is a more chronic condition than the history described here. Furthermore, if this answer referred to SLE flares, these are typically in the context of a history of SLE, which this patient does not have and commonly presents with painful joints, rashes and fatigue. Therefore, this is not the most likely diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old woman has been referred to the clinic. She has had two episodes of shingles in the past 2 months and her GP had noticed persisting lymphadenopathy. The patient currently feels well and there is no past history of note. Examination reveals some petechiae on her back, cervical lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)89 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)48 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Lymphocytes40 × 109/L1.5-3.5 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)116 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Blood filmSmudge cells

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: CLL is the most common adult leukaemia in the Western world. The diagnosis can be discovered incidentally, or patients can have symptoms of anaemia, recurrent bleeding and recurrent infections. Examination can reveal lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly. A full blood count will show a raised WBC with a lymphocytosis. The blood film will show smudge cells, as these are more friable. Immunophenotyping will confirm the diagnosis, with CD19 and CD5 white cell markers likely to be present.

B. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: ALL is unlikely to be the diagnosis given that blast cells have not been found to be present on the blood film.

A. Hairy cell leukaemia: Hairy cell leukaemia is usually associated with a low white blood cell count rather than the mature lymphocytosis seen here.

C. Splenic lymphoma: Primary splenic lymphoma is associated with enlargement of the spleen as is seen here, but is not associated with the marked elevation in white blood cell count.

D. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is associated with peripheral lymphadenopathy and impaired immune function, although the marked elevation in peripheral blood lymphocyte count is not seen.

A 58-year-old woman is admitted for resection of a caecal carcinoma. She is not taking any medications, has no other past medical history, is a non-smoker and drinks little alcohol. Preoperative physical examination is unremarkable, with a blood pressure of 125/85 mmHg, pulse 76/min and regular. BMI is 23.

Preoperative bloods reveal the following:

The operation was uneventful. with no evidence of secondary spread and the patient received 2 units of blood during the procedure. Five days later she was icteric and tired. She is apyrexial, and apart from tenderness around her scar, she tells you that her surgical pain is gradually improving.

Repeat bloods reveal the following:

Which investigation will most likely lead to a confirmed diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Direct antiglobulin test: Delayed transfusion reactions occur 5-10 days after transfusion and are almost invariably delayed haemolytic reactions due to the development of red cell (RBC) allo-antibodies. Clinical features are usually minimal but can include unexplained pyrexia, jaundice or unexplained drop in haemoglobin. Urinalysis shows urobilinogenuria and a blood shows fragile ballooned spherocytes. Diagnosis is confirmed by a direct antiglobulin (Coombs') test that detects the presence of antibody on the RBCs. The test is performed by adding anti-human globulin (AHG) (anti-Ig G and anti-complement) to the patient's washed RBCs. A positive test results in red cell agglutination.

D. Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS): Although blood loss as a result of the procedure may result in a haemoglobin of 60 g/l, the elevated bilirubin suggests that haemolysis as the more likely cause here.

A. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies: Anti-cardiolipin antibodies lead to prolongation of APTT and increased risk of thrombosis, rather than haemolysis.

B. Serum haptoglobin: Haptoglobin is decreased in conditions of haemolysis, although it does not confirm the underlying cause.

C. Reticulocyte count: Reticulocytes are elevated in patients with haemolysis, although they don't indicate the underlying cause.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman is admitted with a swollen left leg which, on venous Doppler, proved to be due to deep venous thrombosis (DVT). She was started on low-molecular weight heparin. The next day, she had an episode of left-sided chest pain and coughed up blood. A ventilation-perfusion scan demonstrated an area of low perfusion.

Five days later (the day after discharge), she developed central chest discomfort and a painful swollen right lower limb.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
White cell count (WCC)12 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)45 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT)30 s25-35 s

What is the likely cause of this new problem?
options: E. Rupture of the right calf muscle
questions.explanation:
D. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: Heparin-induced thrombosis is the most likely diagnosis here, although it occurs much more infrequently with low-molecular weight heparin than with unfractionated heparin. It is prudent not to miss this diagnosis since the treatment is to withhold heparin. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with a new thrombosis is a clinical diagnosis and should be identified when the above clinical features are witnessed, failing which the patient may progress to a fatal thrombosis. Type 1 HIT usually occurs in the first 48-72 h, and the platelet count rarely falls below 100 × 109/L. The platelet count should return to normal over the next 4 days and there is no increased risk of thromboembolism. Type 2 HIT is much rarer and usually occurs 5-10 days after treatment commencement, and the platelet count usually drops below 100 × 109/L to about 50 × 109/L. This case is therefore in keeping with type 2 immune-mediated HIT. Heparin should be stopped and alternative forms of anticoagulation may be required; for advice regarding best management, a haematologist should be consulted. Possible alternative forms of anti-coagulation would include lepirudin, argatroban or danaparoid. With regard to the timing of events, it is likely the PE is related to the original DVT, and the limb thrombosis to the HIT.

C. Ruptured right Baker's cyst: A ruptured Baker's cyst occurs in a patient with pre-existing knee osteoarthritis, and is associated with pain and swelling behind the knee.

A. Spontaneous right limb DVT: Given the timing, five days after commencing low-molecular weight heparin, a new spontaneous DVT is much less likely versus one related to HIT.

B. Cardiac embolism: Cardiac embolism is associated with a cold, pulseless lower limb, rather than the appearance consistent with a DVT seen here.

E. Rupture of the right calf muscle: Calf muscle rupture is associated with pain over the area of muscle where the rupture has occurred, and pain on ankle flexion.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old man is currently undergoing chemotherapy for malignant melanoma which has become disseminated, with spread to his lungs and liver. He has been stable with respect to symptoms over the past few weeks and is expecting to begin the next cycle of chemotherapy in seven days' time. He is very concerned because he suffered a minor knee sprain slipping on some steps but now has a very large left knee haematoma.

Investigations:

Platelets (PLT)152 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.3 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Acquired haemophilia. Acquired haemophilia occurs because of autoantibody inhibitors directed against factor VIII. This leads to quite severe soft tissue haemorrhage, as here, in the face of what may seem like a relatively minor injury. A number of conditions are recognised to cause acquired haemophilia, including autoimmune disease and malignancies such as pancreatic, colon, breast cancers and malignant melanoma. The isolated rise in APTT in the face of a normal platelet count makes platelet-related disorders and vitamin K deficiency much less likely.

B. Chemotherapy-related platelet dysfunction: The normal platelet count seen here counts against an acquired platelet disorder as the cause of this patient's symptoms.

C. Dysfibrinogenaemia: Dysfibrinogenaemia can be associated with both bleeding and an increased risk for thrombosis. Congenital dysfibrinogenaemia is well described and can be associated with major bleeding, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and renal amyloidosis.

D. Vitamin K deficiency: Vitamin K deficiency is associated with a lack of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. This leads to an increased risk for bleeding and prolongation of PT, rather than the picture seen here.

E. Von Willebrand's disease: Acquired von Willebrand's disease is seen more commonly in patients with hypothyroidism, and APTT may be in the normal range. Acquired von Willebrand's disease is seen more commonly in patients with hypothyroidism.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man received unfractionated heparin perioperatively following a routine knee replacement. He was not known to have any cardiovascular risk factors. His blood pressure preoperatively was 130/80 mmHg. He was slow to mobilise, and 4 days post-operatively developed a large wound haematoma and the heparin was stopped. The patient required a transfusion of two units of blood and decompression of the wound. He was not known to have a history of bleeding problems and the operation otherwise was uncomplicated. All preoperative blood tests were normal.

A few days later, the patient is readmitted with right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. Chest X-ray was unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)12 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)17 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
International normalized ratio (INR)1.2< 1.1
Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT)27 s25-35 s
Urea10 mmol/l2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)130 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Liver function testsNormal

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his presentation and blood results?
questions.explanation:
C. Heparin-induced thrombocytopaenia type 2: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is a severe, immune-mediated drug reaction that can occur in any patient exposed to heparin. This includes patients receiving unfractionated heparin (at both full therapeutic doses and low prophylactic doses, including the minute amounts in heparin flushes and on heparin-coated catheters) and those receiving low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH). Antibodies usually develop after a patient has been on heparin for five or more days, but may develop sooner if there has been previous heparin exposure. Despite thrombocytopenia, bleeding is rare. HIT is strongly associated with thrombosis. Thrombo-embolic complications can be venous, arterial or both; these include deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, thrombotic stroke and occlusion of limb arteries.

When HIT is suspected clinically, heparin should be stopped and an alternative anticoagulant commenced, such as danaparoid, lepirudin or argatroban, which do not cross-react with HIT antibodies. Oral anticoagulation with warfarin should not be initiated for longer-term protection from further events until substantial platelet count recovery has occurred. HIT patients who are switched to warfarin alone after the discontinuation of heparin may paradoxically have worsening thrombosis and develop venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis.

The diagnosis of HIT remains a clinical one, supported by confirmatory laboratory testing. The criteria include:
• thrombocytopenia (i.e. a drop in the platelet count to below 100 × 109/L or a drop of >50% from the patient's baseline platelet count)
• the exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia
• the resolution of thrombocytopenia after cessation of heparin.

Regarding the laboratory tests, HIT antibodies can be demonstrated in vitro by functional tests and immunoassays. Functional tests, which measure platelet activity in the presence of the patient's serum and heparin, including heparin-induced platelet aggregation (HIPA) and the serotonin release assay (SRA), are more specific than the immunoassays and are therefore preferred in the diagnosis of HIT.

B. Post-transfusion purpura: Post-transfusion purpura (PTP) is an adverse reaction to a blood transfusion or platelet transfusion that occurs when the body produces allo-antibodies to the introduced platelets' antigens. These allo-antibodies destroy the patient's platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia. PTP usually presents 5-12 days after transfusion, and is therefore not relevant in this case.

A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complex systemic thrombo-haemorrhagic disorder involving the generation of intravascular fibrin and the consumption of procoagulants and platelets. It is seen in association with a number of well-defined clinical situations, including sepsis, major trauma and abruptio placenta. It is associated with prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen, raised fibrin degradation products and thrombocytopenia.

D. Thrombotic thombocytopenic purpura: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a life-threatening multi-system disorder characterised by micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever and renal dysfunction. With the introduction of plasma exchange, the survival rate has improved from approximately 3% prior to the 1960s to 82% now. Platelet transfusions are contraindicated. Fresh-frozen plasma, methylprednisolone and red cell support are all important additional supportive measures.

E. Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), also known as primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura, is defined as isolated thrombocytopenia with normal bone marrow in the absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man is referred to the clinic by his general practitioner. He gives a 12-month history of intermittent night sweats, weight loss, itching and chronic cough. There is no significant reported Gl disturbance. Most recently, he has noticed increasing shortness of breath on climbing the stairs, and has been suffering from an urticarial rash.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Eosinophils3.0 × 109/L or greater on 3 occasions in the last year0.04-0.4 × 109/L
Creatinine (Cr)128 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)Negative
Chest X-ray (CXR)Interstitial infiltrates and small bilateral pleural effusions
Echocardiogram (Echo)Suggestive of restrictive cardiomyopathy
Immunoglobulin E (IgE)Raised

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
B. Hyper-eosinophilic syndrome: This is a myeloproliferative disorder of unknown cause and is rare, occurring most commonly in men in the 30-40-year-old age group. It is associated with a persistent and markedly raised peripheral blood eosinophil count. Lung involvement may occur, as may cardiovascular involvement with fibrosis and restrictive cardiomyopathy, which may lead to mural thrombus formation and considerable morbidity and mortality. There may also be associated angioedema or urticaria. Treatment is with high-dose corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 50 mg, which leads to a response in around 50% of cases). Steroid-sparing agents such as cyclophosphamide or azathioprine may also be of some value. In those patients who carry the FIP1L1/PDGFRA mutation, imatinib is the drug of choice.

A. Churg-Strauss syndrome: 30-40% of patients with Churg-Strauss are positive for PANCA, and they have symptoms of asthma rather than merely the chronic cough seen here. Other features include mononeuritis multiplex, Gl bleeds and glomerulonephritis, which aren't seen here.

C. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia has a much more rapid onset of symptoms, with significant evidence of respiratory failure within 7 days to 1 month from when features first appear.

D. Chronic pulmonary eosinophilia: The extra-pulmonary features seen here are inconsistent versus a diagnosis of chronic pulmonary eosinophilia. Hence this is much less likely to be the underlying diagnosis.

E. Chronic parasitic infection: Chronic parasitic infection is a possible cause of long-term eosinophilia, although there are no pointers in the scenario to suggest exposure to an infective agent. Other features such as Gl disturbance would be expected in helminth infection.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old gentleman presented to the Emergency Department with persistent nose and gum bleeding. He had also noticed some blurred vision and frontal headaches over the past few hours. On examination, he was pale and only his gums were actively bleeding. Neurological examination revealed bilateral horizontal nystagmus on left lateral gaze. Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral decreased visual acuity and retinal haemorrhages.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)8 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)130 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Urea10 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)170 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca2+)2.8 mmol/L2.2-2.7 mmol/l
Phosphate (PO43-)1.77 mmol/l1.1-1.45 mmol/l
Total protein89 g/l60-83 g/l
Albumin30 g/l3.4-5.4 g/l
Prothrombin time (PT)16 s11-14 s
Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT)55 s25-35 s
Peripheral blood smearRouleaux formation

What is the most likely cause for his presentation?
questions.explanation:
D. Hyperviscosity syndrome: Hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS) refers to the clinical sequelae of increased blood viscosity. Increased serum viscosity usually results from increased circulating serum immunoglobulins, and can be seen in such diseases as Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and multiple myeloma. HVS can also result from increased cellular blood components (typically white or red blood cells) in hyperproliferative states such as the leukaemias, polycythaemia and the myeloproliferative disorders. The clinical presentation in HVS consists principally of the triad of mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurologic symptoms. Plasmapheresis is the treatment of choice. This removes the circulating paraproteins and reduces the viscosity.

A. Hypercalcaemia: The neurological symptoms and gum bleeding do not correspond to the clinical presentation of hypercalcaemia (lack of concentration, feeling of 'pins and needles').

B. Bernard-Soulier syndrome: This is caused by a deficiency on the surface of the platelet of the glycoprotein Ib/IX receptor that results in a failure of platelets to stick together in a clump at the site of an injury.

C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: This results in a deficiency in platelet adhesion as a consequence of a deficiency of the surface protein glycoprotein IIb/Illa.

E. Acute kidney disease: Uraemic encephalopathy would not cause the neurological symptoms described in this scenario. Acute kidney disease usually presents with anorexia, nausea, restlessness, drowsiness, diminished ability to concentrate and slowed cognitive functions.

A 64-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department with a history of increasing confusion and headaches. She is noted to have multiple bruises on her shins and arms.

On examination, she has a temperature of 38°C. There is evidence of a petechial rash over her chest. She is tachycardic and has a blood pressure of 110/65 mmHg. There is evidence of bronchial breathing at the right base and 1-cm palpable hepatosplenomegaly.

She is admitted and started on treatment with all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) due to suspected acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) and is covered for concurrent pneumonia with intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav and oral clarithromycin. Initially, her fever settles; however, three days into her admission, she has a fever of 38.5 °C and progressive shortness of breath that gradually worsened. On examination, she has reduced air entry at the bases bilaterally and pitting oedema in the lower limbs bilaterally up to the level of the ankles. Her respiratory rate is 19 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 96%.

What is the best step in management, given the likely diagnosis?
options: E. Switch co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin to piperacillin and tazobactam
questions.explanation:
B. Start high-dose dexamethasone: The combined presentation of a chest infection, high white cell count and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is typical of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which is a malignancy of the bone marrow characterised by a deficiency of mature blood cells in the myeloid cell line and an excess of immature cells called promyelocytes. It is considered a type of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and is classified as the M3 variant in the internationally accepted French-American-British (FAB) classification. Typically, APL is due to a translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 (t(15:17). The break in chromosome 15 disrupts the promyelocytic leukaemia (PML) gene, which encodes a transcription factor. The break in chromosome 17 interrupts the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARa) gene, which regulates myeloid differentiation. The translocation creates a PML-RARa fusion gene, which leads to increased proliferation of promyelocytes.

Treatment of APL differs from that for all other forms of AML. Most APL patients are now treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) which activates the retinoid receptor RAR and causes promyelocytes to differentiate, which deters them from proliferating. ATRA can induce complete remission in most patients with APL by stimulating the APL-blasts to mature. However, ATRA cannot eliminate the leukaemic clone and is, therefore, used in combination with chemotherapy, including an anthracycline drug.

The use of ATRA or arsenic trioxide (ATO) puts patients at risk of differentiation syndrome (DS), a cytokine release syndrome seen in APL after initiation of differentiating agents. The features of DS are respiratory distress, pulmonary infiltrates, fever, weight gain, pleural effusion, renal failure, pericardial effusion, cardiac failure and hypotension. Management involves high-dose systemic steroids, such as dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous (IV) twice a day, alongside ventilatory and blood pressure support. There is no need to discontinue ATRA unless the case is severe.

C. Start IV furosemide: This patient has pleural effusions and some evidence of peripheral fluid overload which could be treated with diuretics. However, the cause here is DS, meaning that treatment with high-dose steroids is most appropriate, rather than treatment with diuretics.

A. Start a 1-unit blood transfusion: This patient's symptoms are most in keeping with differentiation syndrome (DS). There is no evidence of blood loss that would require a blood transfusion and administration of blood products in an individual with evidence of fluid overload should be attempted with caution.

D. Stop ATRA: This patient has developed DS, a cytokine release syndrome seen in APL after initiation of differentiating agents such as ATRA or ATO. There is no need to discontinue ATRA in DS unless the case is severe. Even in severe cases where ATRA is discontinued, steroids need to be administered as DS can be fatal if untreated.

E. Switch co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin to piperacillin and tazobactam: Although this patient has fever and respiratory distress, her chest signs indicate bilateral pleural effusions, with little evidence of worsening chest infection that would require escalation in her antibiotic regimen.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old gentleman complained of a 2-month history of lower back pain. He had been feeling increasingly tired over the last few months and had noted weight loss of 1 stone. He had also noted some tingling in his hands and feet.

On examination, he was found to have gynaecomastia, a palpable 2 cm liver edge and peripheral oedema. There was evidence of loss of pinprick and joint position sense to the mid-shins bilaterally, and diffuse hyperpigmentation of the extremities.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)96 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.4 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)130 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)86 fl80-100 fl
Total protein95 g/L60-83 g/L
Albumin30 g/L35-55 g/l
Fasting Glucose11 mmol/L<5.9 mmol/l
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)7.5 mu/L0.4-5.0 mu/L
Thyroxine (T4)50 nmol/L58-178 nmol/L

What diagnosis best explains the patient's presentation?
options: D. Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes syndrome (POEMS)
questions.explanation:
D. Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes syndrome (POEMS): POEMS syndrome is a rare multi-system disease that occurs in the setting of plasma cell dyscrasia. The pathophysiology of the disease is not known; however, elevated levels of cytokines and growth factors have been implicated. The polyneuropathy associated with POEMS syndrome is a bilateral symmetric disturbance. It involves both motor and sensory nerves, begins distally and has a progressive proximal spread. Associated cranial or autonomic nerves are not involved. Both demyelination and axonal degeneration are noted. The liver, the lymph nodes, and the spleen are the organs most frequently involved. Multiple endocrinopathies have been associated with POEMS syndrome, and most patients have more than one endocrine abnormality. POEMS syndrome is seen in the setting of a plasma cell dyscrasia. Although many plasma cell disorders have been reported in patients with POEMS syndrome, most patients are seen with osteosclerotic myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS). Classic multiple myeloma is not usually associated with the disease.

C. Classical multiple myeloma: This usually presents with bone pain, pathological fractures, weakness, anaemia, infection (often pneumococcal), hypercalcaemia, spinal cord compression or kidney disease. It can also be accompanied by hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurological symptoms).

A. Non Hodgkin's lymphoma: Most patients present with lymphadenopathy. Indermediate- or high-grade lymphomas can also be accompanied by beta symptoms (weight loss, temperature >38°C night sweats).

B. Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia: This is usually accompanied by hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurological symptoms).

E. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (chronic lymphoid leukaemia, CLL) present with a wide range of symptoms and signs. Onset is insidious, and it is not unusual for CLL to be discovered incidentally after a blood cell count is performed for another reason; 25-50% of patients will be asymptomatic at time of presentation. Other signs include lymphadenopathy, hepatospenomegaly, petechiae due to low platelet count, and pallor due to anaemia.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic. He had a recent diagnosis of DVT following a long-haul flight, for which he has completed three months of anticoagulation. There is no significant past medical history. Investigations show that he has a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation.

What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's condition?
options: A. Advise on compression stockings to be worn daily
B. Commence low-dose aspirin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent thrombosis
C. Discuss lifestyle modifications to reduce thrombotic risk factors
D. Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant
E. Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with warfarin
questions.explanation:
C. Discuss lifestyle modifications to reduce thrombotic risk factors: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited cause of thrombophilia. Current guidelines state that, following a DVT, patients with factor V Leiden should be managed as those without thrombophilia. Therefore, the decision to continue anticoagulation should not be based on the presence of factor V Leiden alone. To reduce the risk of further thrombotic events, lifestyle modifications, such as smoking cessation, weight management, regular exercise and avoiding prolonged immobility, are important and should be discussed with the patient.

E. Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with warfarin: For the same reasons as initiating a lifelong direct-acting oral anticoagulant, patients with factor V Leiden do not necessarily need long-term anticoagulation based on the presence of thrombophilia alone. When considering the need for ongoing anticoagulation, a full account of their past medical history and risk factors for thrombosis should be considered. As this patient had a provoked DVT, without any other known risk factors, lifestyle modifications should be the initial management.

A. Advise on compression stockings to be worn daily: Compression stockings reduce the risk of DVT and are given as prophylaxis, particularly for patients who are at a higher risk of thrombosis. However, it is not indicated as a form of long-term management for patients with a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation.

B. Commence low-dose aspirin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent thrombosis: Low-dose aspirin is typically used to reduce the risk of thrombosis in patients with significant risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease. It is not typically recommended for primary prevention in patients with a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation.

D. Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant: In patients with factor V Leiden, initiating long-term anticoagulation should be based on the entire clinical picture, including the risk of further thrombosis and whether the patient had a provoked or an unprovoked DVT. In this case, the patient had a provoked DVT. Therefore, initiating long-term anticoagulation is not indicated at this stage. Rather, lifestyle modifications should be given to reduce the risk of further thrombosis.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a routine physical examination. He has a history of heavy alcohol use but reports no recent symptoms. He takes no regular medications. Physical examination is notable for mild pallor but is otherwise unremarkable. Blood tests reveal the following:

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/l135-175 g/l
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)105 fl80-96 fl
White cell count (WCC)5.5 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)210 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Vitamin B12Normal200-900 pg/ml
FolateLow3-15 ng/ml

What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's macrocytosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Folate deficiency: Folate deficiency is a common cause of macrocytosis, especially in patients with alcohol use, which can impair folate absorption and metabolism. Low folate levels directly correlate with increased red cell volume and macrocytic anaemia.

C. Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism can cause macrocytosis, although this is less common and usually occurs alongside other symptoms of hypothyroidism. The vignette does not suggest hypothyroid symptoms and thyroid function tests were not included, making this less likely.

A. Vitamin B12 deficiency: Vitamin B12 deficiency often leads to macrocytic anaemia. However, the patient's vitamin B12 levels are within the normal range, making this an unlikely cause of his macrocytosis.

D. Myelodysplastic syndrome: Myelodysplastic syndrome can present with macrocytosis, particularly in older patients. However, there are typically abnormalities in other cell lines, such as anaemia with low WCC or PLT count, or a higher mean corpuscular Hb concentration. Given that this patient's other counts are within the normal range, folate deficiency remains as the most likely diagnosis here.

E. Chronic liver disease: Chronic liver disease can cause macrocytosis due to changes in lipid composition of red cell membranes, but this patient's LFTs are not provided and no other specific signs of liver disease are noted. Although alcohol use is a contributing factor to both liver disease and folate deficiency, the latter is more directly implicated here.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with an 18 h history of a severe headache, right-sided hemiparesis and new-onset grand mal seizures. She denied taking any medication or recreational drugs. She had a temperature of 37.6°C, pulse 120 bpm, sinus rhythm and a blood pressure of 110/80 mmHg.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)64 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)10.0 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)10.0 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
International normalized ratio (INR)1.3< 1.1
Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT)26 s25-35 s
Creatinine (Cr)150 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
Urea10.0 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/L
Bilirubin90 μmol/L1-22 μmol/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)21 u/l10-40 u/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)25 u/l7-55 u/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)3200 u/l140-280 u/L

What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a life-threatening multi-system disorder characterised by micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever and renal dysfunction. With the introduction of plasma exchange, the survival rate has improved from approximately 3% prior to the 1960s to 82% now. Platelet transfusions are contraindicated. Fresh-frozen plasma, methylprednisolone and red cell support are all important additional supportive measures.

A. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), also known as primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura, is defined as isolated thrombocytopenia with normal bone marrow in the absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

B. Disseminated intravascular coagulation: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complex systemic thrombo-haemorrhagic disorder involving the generation of intravascular fibrin and the consumption of procoagulants and platelets. It is seen in association with a number of well-defined clinical situations, including sepsis, major trauma and abruptio placenta. It is associated with prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen, raised fibrin degradation products and thrombocytopenia.

D. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is characterised by acute kidney disease, micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, fever and thrombocytopenia. Diarrhoea and upper respiratory infection are the most common precipitating factors. It is caused by strains of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, especially E. coli O157:H7 carrying the Shigalike toxin.

E. Cocaine abuse: Cocaine is a complex drug that can cause lethal cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular arrhythmias. The exact mechanism of cocaine-related stroke remains unclear, and there are likely to be a number of factors involved. There does not appear to be any direct neurotoxic action, and potential mechanisms involved in cocaine induced stroke include vasospasm, cerebral vasculitis, enhanced platelet aggregation, cardio-embolism and hypertensive surges associated with altered cerebral autoregulation and cerebral blood flow. Cocaine use is associated with both intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage. As with ischaemic stroke, the exact mechanism involved is not fully understood, though may involve cocaine-induced haemodynamic changes in susceptible individuals.

questions.question:
You are called by a general practitioner who wants to discuss a case of transient thrombocytopenia with you. His patient is a 23-year-old woman who presented to him with tiredness; he arranged a routine full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes. The ethylene diaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) sample revealed a platelet count of 40 × 109/L with clumping seen on the film. A repeat citrate sample revealed a count of 150 × 109/L. Her white blood count (WBC), haemoglobin and blood film were all unremarkable.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
D. Do nothing: EDTA-induced platelet clumping is thought to occur in around 0.3% of patients. It is not indicative of any underlying disease but is thought to be due to an antibody present in the sample, which promotes platelet aggregation in the presence of EDTA. The normal platelet count in the presence of a citrated sample (normally used to assess clotting) confirms the diagnosis. Because the platelet count normalises in the citrate sample, there is no indication of an underlying disease.

B. Aspirin: The normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment.

A. Abdominal ultrasound: There is nothing in the history to suggest any significant abnormality, and the normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment or investigation.

C. Bone marrow aspirate: This would be an appropriate investigation if the patient had persistent thrombocytopenia, but as there is evidence of EDTA-induced platelet clumping, no further investigation is required.

E. Oral prednisolone: Glucocorticoids would be a treatment for immune thrombocytopenia. The normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment.

questions.question:
A man aged 62 years is referred to the Haematology Clinic for review. He received a routine blood screen from his general practitioner (GP) that revealed a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (85 mm/h) and a raised immunoglobulin G (IgG) paraprotein band (1.9 g/l). No urinary light chain excretion was detected.

Three years later, he remains well; however, he still has an increased ESR and IgG paraprotein band, though there is still no urinary light chain excretion.

Which of the following diagnoses fit best with this clinical picture?
options: B. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS)
questions.explanation:
B. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS): MGUS occurs in older people and is characterised by the presence of a paraprotein band (immunoglobulin G [IgG] <20 g/l). Patients may be asymptomatic and the condition discovered by chance. Blood count is usually normal, and there is no renal dysfunction. No specific treatment is required. Around 1% of patients with MGUS may progress to myeloma annually. In many patients with disease progression, immunoglobulin (Ig) gene rearrangement can be detected in B lymphocytes before the appearance of myeloma. This suggests that MGUS is a clonal, pre-malignant condition.

C. Myeloma: There is no light chain excretion in the urine that would confirm the diagnosis of myeloma, and no organ involvement (e.g. bone, liver, spleen).

A. Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia: This is one of the malignant monoclonal gammopathies and is a chronic, indolent, lymphoproliferative disorder. It is characterised by the presence of a high level of a macroglobulin (immunoglobulin M [IgM]), elevated serum viscosity and the presence of a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the bone marrow.

D. B-cell lymphoma: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is a collective term for a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative malignancies with differing patterns of behaviour and responses to treatment. Most NHLs (80-85%) are of B-cell origin. There is no distinct paraprotein in the serum electrophoresis, but there may be a diffuse increase in the IgG region.

E. Chronic myeloid leukaemia: Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML), also known as chronic myeloid leukaemia, is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by increased proliferation of the granulocytic cell line without the loss of their capacity to differentiate. It accounts for 20% of all leukaemias affecting adults. Again, there is no distinct paraprotein band on the serum protein electrophoresis and the natural history is not indolent.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man with a background of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of lethargy, nausea and vomiting. He was last seen in the Haematology Outpatient Clinic one week ago after completing his induction regime of chemotherapy. There is no other past medical history of note, and he has no allergies.

On examination, his temperature is 37.8°C with a heart rate of 105 bpm and a BP of 100/70 mmHg. Auscultation of his chest is clear, and his abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness.

Investigations:

InvestigationResults a week agoResults todayNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)88 g/l80 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)44.7 × 109/L44.7 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)71 × 109/L21 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)135 mmol/l142 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/l5.9 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.1 mmol/l16.2 mmol/L1.8-7.1 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)80 μmol/l255 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L
Lactate dehydrogenase300 U/L755 U/L< 250 U/L
Adjusted calcium2.3 mmol/l2.0 mmol/l2.2-2.6 mmol/l
Phosphate1.2 mmol/l1.6 mmol/l0.8-1.5 mmol/L
Uric acid200 μmol/L480 μmol/L200-430 μmol/l
C-reactive protein (CRP)44 mg/L50 mg/l<10 mg/L

Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the definitive treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
D. Rasburicase: This patient has a diagnosis of tumour lysis syndrome, given the history of recent chemotherapy use and the onset of nausea, vomiting, lethargy and significantly deranged electrolytes. The destruction of tumour cells causes the release of intracellular contents into the circulation that, in large quantities, cause acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias and cerebral dysfunction. Tumour lysis syndrome can be classified into clinical and laboratory subtypes. Laboratory tumour lysis syndrome is defined as the presence of two or more metabolic abnormalities: hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia. Clinical tumour lysis syndrome is defined as the presence of one or more clinical manifestations of the disease (eg acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias). A closer look at this patient's laboratory results shows evidence of clinical and laboratory tumour lysis syndrome. Tumour lysis syndrome is an oncological emergency and must be treated promptly. Treatment includes intravenous fluid hydration with isotonic solution and rasburicase. Rasburicase is a recombinant form of the urate oxidase enzyme that transforms uric acid in a more soluble product that is more easily eliminated by the kidney. It is effective in both the treatment and prevention of tumour lysis syndrome.

B. Calcium gluconate: Calcium gluconate is a reasonable management choice, given the combined hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia. However, this treatment is only effective at treating these isolated electrolyte disturbances. Rather, rasburicase is the most definitive management for treating established tumour lysis syndrome.

A. Allopurinol: Allopurinol is used in the prophylaxis of tumour lysis syndrome. However, it is not used in the management of established tumour lysis syndrome which is clear here, given the onset of symptoms and deranged biochemistry results.

C. Hypotonic intravenous fluids: Intravenous fluid administration is important in the prevention and management of tumour lysis syndrome. However, guidelines recommend initiating isotonic solutions, which are better at remaining within the intravascular system. However, hypotonic fluids are able to pass freely into the intracellular spaces and have little impact on supporting the intravascular system and improving glomerular filtration.

E. Urinary alkalinisation: Urinary alkalinisation involves initiating sodium bicarbonate solution to prevent the ionisation of acidic substances and improve renal excretion. This method is typically used for salicylate overdose. However, urinary alkalinisation is not recommended in the management of tumour lysis syndrome.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old patient is 1-month post-allogeneic bone marrow transplantation when her condition deteriorates. She has developed a maculopapular rash on the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet, and has become jaundiced. The patient has also been having bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea and, as a result, has lost weight. She is currently taking ciclosporin.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/l135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)3.4 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Urea9.2 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)112 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Bilirubin79 μmol/L1-22 μmol/l
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)310 u/L30-150 u/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)55 u/l7-55 u/l
Albumin27 g/l35-55 g/l

Which of the following investigations should be ordered to guide treatment of the underlying condition?
options: E. Upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract endoscopy with biopsies
questions.explanation:
B. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR): The patient has acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). This presents within 100 days of an allogeneic bone marrow transplantation with a skin rash (which can progress to erythroderma), liver dysfunction (cholestatic) and involvement of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. It remains a serious cause of mortality and morbidity in bone marrow transplant recipients. Patients are staged according to the severity of involvement of the skin, liver and Gl tract. Initial aggressive treatment with intravenous (IV) corticosteroids is recommended. Anti-T cell antibodies, such as OKT3, have been used in patients with resistant disease, as have rituximab and anti-thymocyte globulin. The diagnosis of GVHD is based primarily on clinical symptoms and manifestations. It is essential that infective causes of patient symptoms are ruled out due to the level of immunosuppression and the fact that identification of infection would change patient management. Therefore, blood, urine and stool cultures and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for cytomegalovirus (CMV), human herpesvirus 6, adenovirus and parvovirus should be ordered for any patient presenting with symptoms of GVHD. Therefore, CMV PCR would be the most appropriate investigation here, as the remaining options are likely to provide more information about the degree of organ involvement of GVHD but would not significantly change management.

A. Autoimmune liver panel: The main hepatobiliary differentials in cases of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) are viral hepatitis, drug-induced hepatotoxicity, veno-occlusive disease of the liver, acalculous cholecystitis and total parenteral nutrition (TPN)-associated cholestasis (if patients are receiving TPN at the time of symptoms). Autoimmune disease of the liver is an unlikely differential in the setting of a recent bone marrow transplantation, not least due to the administration of immunosuppressive medications.

C. Computed tomography (CT) abdomen: In patients with Gl tract involvement of GVHD, computed tomography (CT) abdomen may reveal diffuse colitis or feature of ileus. A CT abdomen may also reveal ascites due to abdominal serositis. However, these features are not specific to GVHD and therefore, their presence on imaging is unlikely to affect the management of the underlying condition.

D. Skin biopsy: As the likely diagnosis in this patient is GVHD, skin biopsy is likely to show a lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis. A tissue biopsy of any of the affected organs in GVHD may be ordered after appropriate laboratory and imaging studies to definitively rule in or out the diagnosis. However, it is important that basic laboratory tests are ordered first in this patient to rule out other diagnoses which would change this patient's management.

E. Upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract endoscopy with biopsies: Chronic GVHD may reveal diagnostic features on upper Gl endoscopy such as oesophageal web, stricture or concentric rings. However, as this patient is suffering from acute GVHD, endoscopy will not be of value here to guide further management.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old gentleman was admitted with right-sided hemiparesis. He was known to be on warfarin for a mitral valve replacement and had been adequately anticoagulated. He was taking furosemide and had recently started taking St John's wort for low mood.

On examination, his pulse was 90 beats/min and regular, and his blood pressure was 150/80 mmHg. Cardiac examination demonstrated normal prosthetic valve sounds with an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The patient had a right-sided hemiparesis and right upper motor neuron VII nerve palsy. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows evidence of a left middle cerebral artery infarction.

What is a possible explanation for the presentation?
options: A. St John's wort is prothrombotic
B. St John's wort reduces the activity of warfarin
C. St John's wort increases platelet aggregation
D. St John's wort increases blood cholesterol levels
E. St John's wort causes vasospasm of the cerebral vessels
questions.explanation:
B. St John's wort reduces the activity of warfarin: St John's wort reduces the INR because it is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450, thus leading to greatly increased warfarin metabolism. Careful monitoring of INR is therefore required if a patient on warfarin wishes to take St John's wort, with up-titration of the warfarin dose according to INR. Ideally an alternative antidepressant should be considered if required, and they should be warned if they do take it that dose reduction of warfarin will be needed when they discontinue the herbal remedy. Echocardiography should also be considered to exclude valve thrombosis, but the immediate priority is assessing and correcting his coagulation status.

A. St John's wort is prothrombotic: It is a liver enzyme inducer.

C. St John's wort increases platelet aggregation: It is a liver enzyme inducer, thus increasing the metabolism of warfarin and decreasing the INR, subsequently predisposing to embolic/thrombotic episodes.

D. St John's wort increases blood cholesterol levels: It is a liver enzyme inducer affecting the metabolism of warfarin.

E. St John's wort causes vasospasm of the cerebral vessels: Cerebral vasospasm can be a complication of subarachnoid haemorrhage. The traditional treatment of subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) from a ruptured cerebral aneurysm included strict blood pressure control, with fluid restriction and antihypertensive therapy when the mean arterial pressure exceeded 130 mm Hg. Studies have shown that the use of calcium channel blockers such as nimodipine or nifedipine may be beneficial for the management of cerebral vasospam.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with aggressive lymphoma is receiving combination chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone. At the start of therapy he had several cervical and axillary lymph nodes, none larger than 2 cm. Several studies of investigational products are available, and he asks you about the terminology of drug development.

In terms of the process of researching a new drug in the oncology setting, which of the following best applies to phase I studies?
options: A. The aim of a phase I study is to assess initial therapeutic activity
B. Phase I studies are conducted once an initial therapeutic effect in humans is demonstrated
C. It is common to combine phase I and II studies
D. Phase I studies usually recruit several hundred patients
E. Phase I studies are classically randomised controlled and double-blinded
questions.explanation:
C. It is common to combine phase I and II studies: Phase I studies study safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, whereas phase II studies study whether there is a therapeutic response. These two phases, in practice, are often combined.

D. Phase I studies usually recruit several hundred patients: Phase I studies study safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in an investigational agent's first usage in human subjects. They are not designed to assess therapeutic response, and patients should be aware of this as part of the consent process. As such, they tend to be small trials with only a few patients recruited to them.

A. The aim of a phase I study is to assess initial therapeutic activity: Phase II studies assess whether or not there is a therapeutic response, whereas phase I studies assess safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (which may include initial hints as to the efficacy of the intervention).

B. Phase I studies are conducted once an initial therapeutic effect in humans is demonstrated: Phase III studies are performed once initial safety and efficacy evaluation is completed, and usually compare the drug with an alternative.

E. Phase I studies are classically randomised controlled and double-blinded: Usually phase III and sometimes phase II trials are randomised controlled trials. Within the oncology trial setting, sponsors do not need to be blinded. They can be privy to all information relating to the trial, including the treatment allocated to patients and their outcomes during the trial.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man presents with headaches, lethargy and severe intractable back pain. He also recently suffered left lower lobe pneumonia. Over the past few days, his problems have significantly worsened and he is now unable to keep any food or fluids down and is vomiting several times during the day.

On examination, his BP is 162/95 mmHg and he looks pale. His pulse is 90/min and regular and there are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin101 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.9 × 109/L4-11 × 109/L
Platelets147 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)142 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)6.0 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine890 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L
Viscosity2.78 mPa/s1.50-1.72 mPa/s
Total protein110 g/l60-80 g/l
Albumin30 g/l35-55 g/l
P-ANCA+
UrineProtein++
USS renal tractBilateral normal-sized kidneys, no obstruction

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Multiple myeloma: Whilst we are not given a serum calcium result here, the clinical history of severe backpain, headaches, lethargy and an episode of sepsis is typical of myeloma. The clinical findings of decreased serum albumin, marked elevation in total protein and proteinuria further support the diagnosis. Serum electrophoresis is likely to reveal a paraprotein band. Slightly confusingly, p-ANCA positivity is associated with both multiple myeloma and vasculitis. A period of dehydration associated with the pneumonia may well have been enough to precipitate acute on chronic kidney disease here.

B. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with positive c-ANCA. P-ANCA positivity is associated with multiple myeloma.

C. Polyarteritis nodosa: Polyarteritis nodosa may be associated with renal vasculitis, although significant proteinuria would be unexpected in the absence of evidence of haematuria.

D. Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease: Anti-GBM disease is associated with pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis, rather than the picture here of acute on chronic kidney disease with proteinuria.

E. Waldenström's macrogammaglobulinaemia: Waldenström's is associated with an IgM paraprotein band as well as features of hyperviscosity syndrome and cryoglobulinaemia. Although this patient has headaches which may fit with Waldenstrom's, counting against this is the back pain which suggests bony deposits of myeloma, and of course bone involvement isn't classically described in Waldenstrom's.

questions.question:
A 71-year-old man is found to be anaemic on routine testing when he changes to a new general practitioner (GP). He has hypertension which is treated with lisinopril and amlodipine and has complained of back pain for the last 6 months.
