On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 132/72 while his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. There is mild bilateral pitting oedema of the ankles.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)108 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)11.1 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)187 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/l135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.3 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)105 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L
Albumin28 g/l35-55 g/l
Total protein61 g/l60-83 g/l

Which of the following would fit best with a diagnosis of symptomatic myeloma?
options: B. Femoral and lumbar spine lytic lesions on skeletal survey
D. 8% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow sampling
questions.explanation:
B. Femoral and lumbar spine lytic lesions on skeletal survey: Criteria for diagnosis of symptomatic myeloma were drawn up in 2015 and are listed below:
Symptomatic myeloma diagnosis criteria:
• Monoclonal plasma cells in bone marrow (aspirate or trephine) ≥10%
• Serum paraprotein ≥30 g/l (if IgM paraprotein exclude lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma).
• Evidence of end-organ damage that can be attributed to myeloma. This is termed myeloma-related organ or tissue injury (ROTI) and commonly called the CRAB criteria:
• C: hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca²+ >0.25 mmol/l above normal or >2.75 mmol/l)
• R: renal impairment (no other cause)
• A: anaemia (Hb <100 g/L or more than 20 g below normal, not due to other causes)
• B: bone lesions (lytic lesions or osteoporosis).

A. Creatinine 105 μmol/L: It is within the normal range and thus would be unusual in symptomatic myeloma.

C. Hb of 108 g/l: It would be insufficient to meet the diagnostic criteria for symptomatic myeloma.

D. 8% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow sampling: This is more consistent with monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance - in myeloma, the clonal plasma cells should be >10% on bone marrow biopsy.

E. Urine negative for protein: Proteinuria is a feature of symptomatic multiple myeloma.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of epistaxis, which settles with conservative management. Apparently, she has had a recent flu-like illness.

On examination, she has a number of petechiae and some bruising where she has taken knocks or bangs to her legs. She is on no significant medication and has an unremarkable past medical history. It is understood that her aunt had a splenectomy as a young adult. She is offered treatment with steroids, but she declines because she has heard that there are potential side effects.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.0 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)16.0 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)139 mmol/l135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.0 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)105 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: D. Reinforce that prednisolone 60 mg daily is the only effective treatment
questions.explanation:
C. Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy: This patient has idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Over recent years, a familial propensity for the development of ITP has been identified, although the particular gene for susceptibility is yet to be identified. Steroid therapy is often offered first-line to treat ITP. A second-line option is intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, which, at the cellular level, blocks the binding sites for autoantibodies that are causing platelet destruction.

D. Reinforce that prednisolone 60 mg daily is the only effective treatment: First-line treatment involves the use of high-dose corticosteroids. Alternative options also exist, including intravenous immunoglobulin, which would be the next most appropriate treatment for an acute presentation. Second-line treatments include rituximab and/or splenectomy.

A. Azathioprine 100 mg daily: Azathioprine is a potential steroid-sparing agent in the treatment of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in patients who are unable to significantly reduce their dose of prednisolone without a fall in platelet count.

B. Platelet transfusion: Platelet transfusions may be required for uncontrolled haemorrhage, although they do not reduce the underlying autoantibody burden resulting in platelet destruction. They are not therefore the initial intervention of choice.

E. Splenectomy: Splenectomy is required for patients who do not respond to immune intervention for treatment of thrombocytopenia.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic with a 4-week history of increased fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. She complains of feeling frequently tired and has been unable to attend her university lectures due to exhaustion and recurrent chest infections. There is no past medical history of note, and she takes no regular medications.

On examination, she is afebrile. Her heart rate is 101 bpm and regular with a BP of 122/70mmHg. Auscultation of her chest is clear with oxygen saturation of 94% on air. There is palpable non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy and a marginally palpable liver edge.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultsNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)78 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)24.7 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)20 × 109/l150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.1 mmol/l1.8-7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)80 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
C-reactive protein (CRP)4 mg/L<10 mg/l
Bone marrow aspirateHypercellularity with 25% lymphoblast infiltration

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is an indicator of poor prognosis?
questions.explanation:
C. T(9:22) translocation: This patient has a likely diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia given the acute onset of lethargy and recurrent infections, combined with the examination findings of cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatomegaly. The blood results are also suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and an elevated white cell count with predominant blast cells on bone marrow aspirate. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a common childhood malignancy that generally has a good prognosis. However, there are markers of poor prognosis that include the presence of the T(9:22) translocation that codes for the Philadelphia chromosome. The Philadelphia chromosome is linked to increased resistance to standard chemotherapeutic regimes in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and, therefore, predicts a poorer outcome.

A. Female sex: Female sex is a good prognostic indicator in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. In contrast, male sex is a poor prognostic marker.

B. T(12;21) translocation: The t(12;21) translocation, which is responsible for the TEL-AML1 (ETV6-RUNX1) fusion gene, is common in childhood ALL but rare in adults. It confers a good risk profile.

D. WCC below 30 × 10^9/L: A WCC of under 30 × 109/L is a good prognostic indicator for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Poor prognostic markers for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia include over 30 × 109/L or over 100 × 109/L for B- and T-cell lineages, respectively.

E. Young age: Young age is a good prognostic indicator for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. In adults, those aged over 35 years are considered to have a higher risk of poorer outcomes.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman presents with a 12 hour history of a sudden loss of power in the left arm. She is previously fit and well, smokes five cigarettes daily and is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her grandfather had a stroke in his eighties, and she has five siblings who are well.

Examination shows increased tone and brisk reflexes in the left arm. There is a 12 cm splenomegaly. Computed tomography of the head is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)123 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)18.5 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)1035 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L

A blood film shows a left shift with markedly increased platelets, which vary significantly in size (anisothrombia). Bone marrow shows a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Essential thrombocythaemia with cerebrovascular accident
B. Antiphospholipid syndrome with reactive thrombocytosis
C. Cerebral lupus with reactive thrombocytosis
questions.explanation:
D. Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML): The history is compatible with a cerebrovascular accident, and the high platelet count is likely to be the cause. Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (a myeloproliferative disorder) usually manifests with thrombocytosis at presentation, usually with a raised white cell count that is grossly left-shifted (where promyelocytes, metamyelocytes and myelocytes are all visible on the peripheral blood). There is usually marked splenomegaly and the bone marrow is nearly always positive for the Philadelphia chromosome (the abnormally small chromosome 22 is the 'Philadelphia' chromosome). The absolute basophil count is often increased in myeloproliferative disorders.

A. Essential thrombocythaemia with cerebrovascular accident: Essential thrombocythaemia can present with splenomegaly, but where the Philadelphia chromosome is found the disease is always classified as chronic myeloid leukaemia. There would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in essential thrombocythaemia.

B. Antiphospholipid syndrome with reactive thrombocytosis: Platelet counts are characteristically low in anti-phospholipid syndrome, but are high in all the myeloproliferative disorders such as CML. Also, there would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in anti-phospholipid syndrome.

C. Cerebral lupus with reactive thrombocytosis: Central lupus usually presents with low platelets and pancytopenia. It can give rise to strokes, seizures or changes to the mental state. There would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in lupus.

E. Acute myeloid leukaemia: Acute myeloid leukaemia occurs when there is a maturational arrest in bone marrow cells early on in their development, leading to a variety of blood test results. These include thrombocytopenia, anaemia and low, high or normal white cell counts. Circulating blasts are seen on a blood film and there is no translocation of chromosomes with AML.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with fever and reduced consciousness. Her past medical history includes type Il diabetes, for which she takes metformin, gliclazide and insulin therapy. She is treated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics and transferred to the Medical Ward.

After 48 hours into her admission, the nursing team inform the doctors that her condition has deteriorated. She has a heart rate of 130 bpm and blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. Her temperature remains elevated at 39.1 °C. She is fluid-resuscitated with 4 × 500-ml boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride. Her repeat observations show a heart rate of 120 bpm and blood pressure of 88/62 mmHg.

Repeat investigations:

InvestigationOn admissionTodayNormal value
Haemoglobin144 g/l150 g/L135-175 g/L
White cell count16.1 × 109/L15.2 × 109/L4-11 × 109/L
Platelets406 × 109/L555 × 109/L150-450 × 109/L
Creatinine125 μmol/L335 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
C-reactive protein340 mg/l310 mg/l<10 mg/L
Glucose12.2 mmol/L8.1 mmol/L4-7 mmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: E. Speak to Microbiology about escalating antibiotic regime
questions.explanation:
D. Noradrenaline infusion: Initiating noradrenaline therapy would be appropriate here. This patient is showing signs of septic shock with fever, tachycardia and hypotension. Patients who are unresponsive to 2 litres of fluid resuscitation should be discussed with the Intensive Care Unit for consideration of vasopressor support to help maintain a stable blood pressure.

B. Haemofiltration: Haemofiltration would not be appropriate, as although this patient shows signs of impaired renal function, this is likely secondary to reduced organ perfusion secondary to septic shock. Indications for haemofiltration include refractory hyperkalaemia and acidosis, uraemia and fluid overload. These features are not seen in this patient.

A. Dopamine infusion: In patients who remain hypotensive despite adequate fluid resuscitation, appropriate antibiotic choice and noradrenaline, the addition of a second or third agent to noradrenaline may be required (eg adrenaline, dobutamine, vasopressin), with little data to support agent selection. Some studies showed improved survival with dobutamine.

C. Intravenous hydrocortisone: Routine use of glucocorticoids should not be used in patients with sepsis. Hydrocortisone may have a role in the presence of severe sepsis not responding to adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.

E. Speak to Microbiology about escalating antibiotic regime: This patient has signs of ongoing sepsis, as evidenced by her raised inflammatory markers and ongoing hypotension. Although it is possible that the initial antibiotic regime is inadequate in controlling her infection, this patient currently has signs of septic shock which must be addressed first. Therefore, initiating a noradrenaline infusion takes priority over escalating antibiotics with Microbiology.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old man presents to the Acute Medical Unit with symptomatic anaemia, requiring a blood transfusion. Ten minutes after the transfusion is started, the emergency bell is called as the nurses fear that he is having a reaction to the transfusion.

On arrival, the patient complained of feeling faint and breathless. Examination shows an unwell, pale and clammy patient with a heart rate of 120 bpm, BP is 70 mmHg systolic, respiratory rate of 35 breaths per minute, temperature of 38.9°C and GCS score 13/15. The patient's blood group is group A rhesus-negative; the blood transfusion is group O rhesus-negative.

What is the most likely cause of this patient's deterioration?
options: A. Acute intravascular haemolysis due to inappropriate ABO crossmatching
B. Acute transfusion reaction due to donor cytokines
C. Anaphylactic reaction to blood products
D. Bacterial contamination of the unit of blood
questions.explanation:
D. Bacterial contamination of the unit of blood: Bacterial contamination is a possibility, although this is very rare with red cell transfusions and more common with platelet transfusions (which are stored at room temperature). However, if such contaminated blood is stored for a few days at room temperature (eg platelets) or for a few weeks at refrigerated temperature (eg red cells), bacteria may grow and elaborate endotoxin, which is a major adverse factor in such reactions and drives the acute presentation seen here.

C. Anaphylactic reaction to blood products: Anaphylaxis to blood products should always be considered for patients presenting with an acute reaction, particularly if tachycardic and hypotensive, with difficulty in breathing. However, an anaphylactic reaction is normally an immediate process and is less likely to be seen associated with a fever. For this reason, contaminated blood products are more likely.

A. Acute intravascular haemolysis due to inappropriate ABO crossmatching: Immunoglobulin M anti-A and anti-B antibodies cause acute haemolytic transfusion reactions, and as little as 4 ml of transfused ABO-incompatible blood can be fatal. The labelling of the blood as O rhesus-negative means that an acute transfusion reaction should not be seen.

B. Acute transfusion reaction due to donor cytokines: When patients donate blood at the time of viral infection, increased levels of inflammatory cytokines may be present in the donated unit. These usually cause mild pyrexia rather than the acute symptoms seen here.

E. Transfusion-related acute lung injury: Transfusion-related acute lung injury is associated with acute-onset non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It is thought to be related to donor antibodies to human leukocyte antigens, which drive neutrophil activation. The features seen here are inconsistent with non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema where infiltration of the lung fields would be expected.

questions.question:
A 78-year-old man presents with sudden deterioration of vision in his left eye, with no eye pain. There are flame haemorrhages in one quadrant on retinal examination. He has a history of hypertension and is awaiting investigations for anaemia; recent haemoglobin is 105 g/l.

What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
A. Branch retinal vein occlusion: Patients often complain of a sudden painless decrease of vision in the affected eye. Some patients may complain of a scotoma. The affected area of the retina has flame shaped haemorrhages. Risk factors for retinal vein occlusion include systemic hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperviscosity syndromes. Some inflammatory (e.g. sarcoidosis) and thrombophilic conditions (e.g. SLE) may also be involved. Management involves screening for risk factors and anticoagulation. Further management depends on which underlying condition has been identified.

C. Central retinal vein occlusion: Patients can be either asymptomatic or present with decreased vision, photophobia and painful or red eyes. Fundoscopy shows tortuosity and dilatation of all branches of the central retinal vein, dot/blot and flame-shaped hemorrhages, throughout all four quadrants and most numerous in the periphery, and optic disc and macular oedema. This tends to be more severe in ischaemic CRVO than non-ischaemic CRVO.

B. Branch retinal artery occlusion: This is usually embolic in aetiology. Patients with branch retinal artery occlusion typically present with acute, unilateral, painless, partial visual loss. The affected area of the retina is usually more pale, with a relative absence of vasculature. Visual field defects may be central or sectoral. Patients may also be asymptomatic. Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, coronary artery disease and history of stroke or transient ischemic attack.

D. Central retinal artery occlusion: This is embolic in aetiology. The most common presenting complaint is an acute, persistent, painless loss of vision in the range of counting fingers to light perception in 90% of patients. Early in the course, the fundus may appear normal. The classic findings of retinal whitening and a cherry red spot are due to opacification of the nerve fibre layer as it becomes oedematous from ischeamia. The fovea is cherry red because it has no overlying nerve fibre layer. This finding may take hours to develop, and the oedema is associated with a worse visual prognosis. Over the course of about a month, the inner retina becomes atrophic as the swelling resolves.

E. CMV retinitis: Presenting symptoms vary depending on the location of retinal involvement. Posterior lesions present with diminished visual acuity. More peripheral lesions initially can be asymptomatic. Floaters often are noted if significant vitreitis is present. The eye usually is white and quiet. In immunocompromised individuals, CMV most commonly presents as a viral necrotising retinitis with a characteristic ophthalmoscopic appearance.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old white man is referred by his general practitioner (GP) with cellulitis of his right leg that has been difficult to treat with oral antibiotics. The patient has been experiencing increased fatigue and breathlessness. He drinks a glass of wine at the weekends and is a non-smoker. Apart from childhood asthma, he is well and on no regular medication.

On examination: Pale conjunctivae and multiple bruises over all four limbs. There is hepatosplenomegaly and cellulitis of the right leg.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)82 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)3.0 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/l.
Platelets (PLT)95 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)83 fl76-98 fl
Bone marrow aspirateDry tap
Bone marrow biopsyCells with a 'fried egg' appearance
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase stain (TRAP)strongly positive

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Hairy cell leukaemia: Hairy cell leukaemia is a B-lymphocyte disorder. The abnormal cell has hair-like cytoplasmic projections. Infiltration of the bone marrow leads to pancytopenia and patients have hepatosplenomegaly. The abnormal cells are strongly positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase stain (TRAP). Infiltration of the bone marrow leads to a dry tap on attempted aspiration, and a bone marrow biopsy reveals cells that are said to have the characteristic 'fried egg' appearance. Purine analogues and interferon have been used for treatment, and occasionally splenectomy has been required.

Stains:
• TRAP: tends to be positive in hairy cell leukaemia
• Sudan black B stain and myeloperoxidase: tends to be positive in acute myeloblastic leukaemia
• Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase stain (TDT): tends to be positive in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
• LAP: tends to be raised in polycythemia rubra vera and myelofibrosis; tends to be low in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

A. Chronic myeloid leukaemia: CML is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by the proliferation of the precursors for white blood cells, but these precursors retain the ability to differentiate. Symptoms tend to be chronic and the blood profile shows an increased (++) white cell count, with a low or normal haemoglobin and a variable platelet count.

C. Myelodysplasia: Myelodysplasia occurs mainly in the elderly and presents with anaemia, infection or bleeding due to pancytopenia. Serial blood counts show evidence of increasing bone marrow failure and the bone marrow shows increased cellularity. Patients with <5% blasts in the bone marrow are managed conservatively, 'gentle' chemotherapy is used in patients with high white blood cell counts and intensive chemotherapy is usually reserved for patients under the age of 60 years. Transformation into AML occurs in around 30% of patients. Bone marrow biopsy revealing cells that are said to have the characteristic 'fried egg' appearance is characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia.

D. Myelofibrosis: Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is one of the chronic myeloproliferative disorders, which are collectively characterised by clonal proliferation of myeloid cells with variable morphologic maturity and haematopoietic efficiency. Splenomegaly is a marked feature. Bone marrow biopsy is necessary to demonstrate fibrosis. Some degree of fibrosis is seen in almost all patients; the fibrosis is typically extensive and visualised better with a silver stain (reticulin) or a trichrome stain (mature collagen). Bone marrow sinusoids are expanded and there is intravascular haematopoiesis. The fibrosis is generally associated with atypical megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and thickening and distortion of the bony trabeculae (osteosclerosis).

E. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: The most noteworthy laboratory abnormality found in CLL is lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood and bone marrow. Although the absolute blood lymphocyte threshold for diagnosing CLL has been placed at >5000/microl (5 × 109/L) B lymphocytes, a significant proportion of patients presents with counts as high as 100,000/microl (100 × 109/l). The peripheral blood smear of patients with CLL demonstrates a lymphocytosis. The leukemic cells are typically small, mature-appearing lymphocytes with a dense nucleus, partially aggregated (clumped) chromatin and lacking discernible nucleoli. There is a narrow border of clear to slightly basophilic cytoplasm. The blood film in this scenario is not that of CLL. Bone marrow biopsy revealing cells that are said to have the characteristic 'fried egg' appearance' is characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia, and therefore CLL is an incorrect option.

questions.question:
A 57-year-old man is referred to hospital by his General Practitioner (GP). Previously well, he gives a history of progressive weakness and breathlessness on exertion over a two week period. He is also complaining of symptoms of indigestion.

On examination, he is pale and tachycardic. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. His heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear.

He brings along with him results of blood tests conducted by the GP:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)83 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.2 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)410 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)69 fl80-100 fl
Peripheral smearRBCs hypochromic and microcytic, target cells +, pencil cells +, WBC and platelet morphology normal

Which one of the following would you consider the most useful test to measure?
options: A. Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)
D. Hb electrophoresis and Hb H preparation
questions.explanation:
B. Serum ferritin: This patient is most likely to have iron-deficiency anaemia due to gastrointestinal blood loss. Hypo-ferritinaemia confirms iron deficiency and is the preferred screening test. Ferritin levels may be falsely elevated in acute inflammatory states (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant). Stool for occult blood is a relatively insensitive test of gastrointestinal bleeding. Malabsorption, hookworm infestation and chronic haematuria may also result in iron deficiency. Other causes of microcytosis include haemoglobinopathy (in certain ethnic groups), anaemia of chronic disease (normal/high ferritin levels), lead poisoning (check urine and blood lead levels) and myelodysplastic syndromes with ringed sideroblasts.

A. Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC): In order to properly understand a value for TIBC, one also must know the serum iron, the percentage transferrin saturation and the individual clinical situation. In modern laboratory testing, serum ferritin levels are generally accepted as reliable single indicators of the presence of iron deficiency.

C. Blood lead level: Acute lead poisoning can cause anaemia through haemolysis, accompanied by haemoglobinuria. There is no evidence in this scenario which would support this diagnosis. Symptoms in chronic lead poisoning usually occur with blood levels greater than 50 μg/dl.

D. Hb electrophoresis and Hb H preparation: Haemoglobinopathy is one cause of microcytosis, but it is not the commonest and it is usually discovered earlier in life.

E. Liver function tests: There is no evidence of liver disease from the history and clinical examination, and therefore liver function testing would not be essential for the diagnosis.

questions.question:
An 89-year-old woman is an inpatient recovering from community-acquired pneumonia. She is on apixaban for atrial fibrillation and has been put on intravenous ampicillin since admission 48 hours ago. While on the ward, she falls and hits her head. A computed tomography (CT) head shows evidence of a subdural haemorrhage which has caused a midline shift.

What is the most appropriate management?
options: C. Oral vitamin K 5 mg or intravenous (IV) vitamin K 0.5-1 mg
D. Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X
E. Stop apixaban and repeat CT head after 24 hours to monitor for bleed expansion
questions.explanation:
D. Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X: Prothrombin complex concentrate is extremely useful for rapidly reversing over-anticoagulation. It is used if there is a life-threatening bleed in a patient taking apixaban, eg following an acute large subdural haemorrhage.

A. Cryoprecipitate 10 units: Cryoprecipitate contains higher levels of factor VIII and fibrinogen. Its use is therefore limited mainly to the treatment of dysfibrinogenaemia or hypofibrinogenaemia.

B. Fresh frozen plasma 15 ml/kg: Fresh frozen plasma at a dose of 15 ml/kg is unlikely to raise coagulation factors above 20%. Higher doses, while more likely to correct adequately, can cause fluid overload. Fresh frozen plasma is not virally inactivated and can cause transfusion complications such as transfusion-related acute lung injury. As such, other options for acute reversal of anticoagulation are preferred.

C. Oral vitamin K 5 mg or intravenous (IV) vitamin K 0.5-1 mg: Vitamin K is appropriate for patients who are taking warfarin therapy and require reversal of their anticoagulation.

E. Stop apixaban and repeat CT head after 24 hours to monitor for bleed expansion: A subdural haemorrhage in a patient taking apixaban is an indication for urgent reversal of anticoagulation.

questions.question:
A confused 68-year-old man was brought to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of severe headaches, blurred vision and spontaneous gum bleeding. Prior to his acute presentation, he had been generally unwell for several months with malaise and weight loss.

On examination, he was drowsy and had widespread lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen. Heart sounds were normal and his chest was clear to auscultation. Ophthalmoscopy revealed several retinal haemorrhages. There were no focal neurological signs.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)3.5 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)130 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)135 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)170 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)96 fl76-98 fl
Urea7.2 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)90 mm/hour1-20 mm/hour
Blood filmRouleaux formation

Serum immunoglobulins tests reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Immunoglobulin A (IgA)3.5 g/l1.0-4.0 g/l
IgG10.0 g/l5-16 g/l
IgM22.0 g/l0.5-2.0 g/l

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia: This man has a hyperviscosity syndrome, which occurs when the plasma viscosity rises to a level at which the micro-circulation is impaired (typically >5). Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia is the most common cause of this. Waldenstrom's is a lymphoplasmacytoid malignancy, which tends to occur in older men. There is a recently identified genetic component with a high percentage of patients carrying the MYD88 gene. It usually presents with peripheral lymph node enlargement, enlarged spleen and symptoms of bone marrow infiltration, and is associated with an IgM paraprotein. The high circulating levels of IgM paraprotein form aggregates therefore increase the viscosity of the blood, leading to hyperviscosity syndrome. Criteria for diagnosis of Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) include:
1. IgM monoclonal gammopathy that excludes chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and Mantle cell lymphoma
2. Evidence of anaemia, systemic symptoms, hyperviscosity, enlarged lymph nodes or hepatomegaly orand/or splenomegaly that can be attributed to an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder.
Treatment is with alkylating agents or doxorubicin-containing regimes. Plasmapheresis is used for hyperviscosity due to IgM levels. Less common causes include myeloma (immunoglobulin A (IgA) or IgM paraprotein), polycythaemia or leukaemia (leucostasis).

B. Multiple myeloma: Although hyperviscosity syndrome is occasionally present with multiple myeloma, most patients present with bone pain, pathological fractures, signs of hypercalcaemia, kidney disease and anaemia. IgM multiple myeloma can sometimes be difficult to distinguish from WM, but the systemic symptoms usually point towards one or the other.

A. Tuberculous meningitis: This patient has no history of exposure to tuberculosis. TB meningitis is difficult to diagnose. It usually spreads from another organ (e.g. lung) to form micro-abscesses in the meninges, and it has an insidious onset. Fevers and headaches would present early on, but later symptoms such as confusion, drowsiness and malaise arise.

C. Herpes simplex encephalitis: Usually as a result of herpes simplex type 1 in adults, this presents with signs affecting the temporal and frontal lobes; these include confusion, personality change, drowsiness and headache. There may be seizures. This pattern of symptoms does not correlate with the patient in the question.

E. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: CLL has an insidious onset and is often discovered incidentally. Those with presenting symptoms may have enlarged lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, fatgue, night sweats and recurrent infections. The blood film would show smudge cells, large atypical lymphocytes and pro-lymphocytes. WCC is usually high with a high number of lymphocytes, unlike the patient in this scenario who has low WCC.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with breathlessness. He had a bone marrow transplant for acute myeloid leukaemia four months ago and needs regular blood transfusions. He thinks that he might be anaemic now and is asking for a transfusion to be arranged.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)73 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)3.1 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)103 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Neutrophils1.0 × 109/L2.5-7.58 × 109/L
Blood filmUnremarkable
Coombs' testNegative
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) bone marrow donor statusNegative
CMV bone marrow recipient pretransplant statusNegative

What type of blood should be arranged?
options: A. Two units of ABO-matched blood from a family member
B. Two units of CMV-negative crossmatched blood
C. Two units of human leukocyte antigen-matched blood from a family member
D. Two units of irradiated, CMV-negative red cells
E. Two units of irradiated red cells
questions.explanation:
E. Two units of irradiated red cells: Irradiated blood is indicated in patients with cellular immunodeficiency post-stem cell transplant, those on purine analogue therapy (eg fludarabine), and those with Hodgkin's disease and congenital immunodeficiencies. It is to prevent engraftment by viable T lymphocytes in the donor and causing transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Irradiation of blood products does not affect their quality. Patients should be informed that they need irradiated blood products and given an information card. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a transfusion-transmitted infection that can be fatal in stem cell transplant recipients. Transmission of CMV has dropped markedly with the advent of universal leukodepletion of all blood products. There is a reasonable field of evidence that suggests, in patients who underwent haemopoietic stem cell transplantation, CMV-negative red cells do not lead to any reduction in transmission of CMV, when compared to irradiated products which are not known to be CMV-negative.

C. Two units of human leukocyte antigen-matched blood from a family member: Non-cytomegalovirus (CMV)-screened blood runs the risk of transmission of CMV, and lack of irradiation runs the risk of the unit containing viable white blood cells which could initiate a graft-versus-host disease response.

A. Two units of ABO-matched blood from a family member: Because of previous transfusions, the likelihood of mismatching and a subsequent transfusion reaction is very high so this would not be appropriate for this patient.

B. Two units of CMV-negative crossmatched blood: This would not be appropriate as it runs the risk of human leukocyte antigen mismatch and the presence of T cells in the donor.

D. Two units of irradiated, CMV-negative red cells: There are several trials that demonstrate that there is no advantage to the use of CMV-negative products vs irradiated CMV-positive products. These products are in short supply and should be saved for use elsewhere such as in elective transfusions during pregnancy.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old woman is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic for a follow-up appointment. She has a diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and has recently completed a cycle of consolidation therapy. For the last week, she has noticed a tingling sensation in her fingers and toes.

On examination, there is reduced sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution over her upper and lower limbs. Her cranial nerves are intact.

What is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
E. Vincristine: This patient has presented with tingling in her fingers and toes combined with reduced sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution. This is suggestive of peripheral neuropathy. Of the chemotherapeutic agents used to treat acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, vincristine is the most common agent causing peripheral neuropathy. Vincristine is associated with a painless peripheral neuropathy, and other side effects include constipation and jaw pain.

D. PEG-asparaginase: PEG-asparaginase disrupts protein synthesis in tumour cells and has a number of side effects including pancytopenia, hypersensitivity reactions, hepatoxicity, cerebral toxicity and pancreatitis. However, peripheral neuropathy is not common.

A. Cytarabine: Cytarabine interferes with pyrimidine synthesis with side effects including alopecia, pancytopenia and gastrointestinal upset. Peripheral neuropathy is not a common side-effect of this medication.

B. Doxorubicin: Doxorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent associated with myocardial toxicity. There are a variety of other side effects including pancytopenia and mucositis. However, it is not a common cause of peripheral neuropathy.

C. Mercaptopurine: Mercaptopurine is an immunosuppressant used in the maintenance phase of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and other inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease. Common side effects include bone marrow suppression and hepatic dysfunction. However, peripheral neuropathy is not common.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant pain and swelling of her abdomen over the course of the past week. She is normally completely well, and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. She takes an occasional glass of wine and is a non-smoker and admits to drug use on two occasions as a student.

On examination, her blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg and her pulse is 82 bpm and regular. She has moderate ascites and has a tender liver edge in the right upper quadrant. There is mild jaundice.

Investigations:

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)9.2 × 109/L4-11 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)203 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.3 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 mmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)132 U/L5-30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)178 U/L30-130 IU/L
Bilirubin32 mmol/l2-17 μmol/l
Prothrombin time (PT)17.3 s10.6-14.9 s
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)48.2 s22-41 s

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Hepatic vein thrombosis: There are a number of clues to the underlying diagnosis here - the acute nature of the hepatic decompensation, use of the oral contraceptive pill, and prolonged APTT-raising the possibility of underlying anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome. The prolonged PT is consistent with hepatic dysfunction. Ascitic tap looking for high protein content and ultrasound scanning are the investigations of choice. Local thrombolysis and venous stenting have been attempted in specialist centres. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be required long term for patients with persistent symptoms of hepatic decompensation.

A. Autoimmune hepatitis: Autoimmune hepatitis is more likely to present with chronic lethargy and itching, rather than the acute presentation here. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies and anti-LKM1 antibodies are frequently seen in patients with autoimmune hepatitis, and high-dose prednisolone is the intervention of choice.

C. Hepatitis A: Hepatitis A is associated with a prodromal flu-like illness, often accompanied by diarrhoea. A marked elevation in transaminases, consistent with hepatocellular degeneration, is seen.

D. Hepatitis B: Although this patient does have a history of injecting drug abuse, acute presentation with hepatic decompensation would be very unusual. The condition is diagnosed either with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) on routine testing or when patients present with symptoms consistent with chronic cirrhosis.

E. Hepatitis C: Like hepatitis B, hepatitis C presents with evidence of chronic liver disease or with abnormal LFTs discovered on routine testing, rather than the acute presentation here.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old white woman presents to a locum GP to find out the results of some blood investigations performed by her own GP. She was found to have splenomegaly on a routine examination when she visited her GP, with feelings of excessive tiredness and fatigue. Her blood film had shown elevated basophils and eosinophils with poikilocytes and normoblasts.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)38.0 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)119 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L

Which diagnosis would fit the above data?
questions.explanation:
B. Chronic myeloid leukaemia: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is one of the myeloproliferative disorders and results from an uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells. It is an acquired abnormality involving the haematopoietic stem cell and a reciprocal chromosomal translocation, resulting in the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome. This chromosome is present in the granulocyte, RBC and platelet precursors of >95% of patients with CML. Poikilocytes are variably shaped erythrocytes. Of the conditions listed, the only one which would cause such a marked elevation of the WCC, thrombocytopenia and mild anaemia is CML.

A. Sideroblastic anaemia: Sideroblastic anaemia is associated with the formation of ring sideroblasts, because of defective incorporation of iron into red blood cells.

C. Polycythaemia rubra vera: PCRV is associated with predominant elevation in haemoglobin, rather than the marked elevation in white count seen here.

D. Essential thrombocythaemia: Essential thrombocythaemia is primarily associated with an increase in platelet count, rather than the increase in white count seen here.

E. Thalassaemia: Thalassaemia would not account for the marked elevation in white count with immature red blood cells seen on the film here.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with progressive fatigue, weight loss and recurrent infections over the past three months. Examination reveals pallor, splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections, as shown in the image below. A bone marrow biopsy confirms the presence of hairy cell leukaemia.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)90 g/l135-175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)2.5 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)70 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L

What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
C. Cladribine: Cladribine, a purine analogue, is the treatment of choice for hairy cell leukaemia. It induces durable remissions in most patients by targeting hairy cells selectively. Hairy cell leukaemia is a rare B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterised by pancytopenia, splenomegaly and characteristic 'hairy cells' on peripheral smear.

D. Imatinib: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukaemia and other cancers, but has no role in the management of hairy cell leukaemia.

A. Rituximab: Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, is used for hairy cell leukaemia in cases of relapse or refractory disease but is not first-line therapy.

B. Splenectomy: Splenectomy was historically used in the management of hairy cell leukaemia to control symptoms of splenomegaly. However, with the advent of effective chemotherapeutic agents, it is now rarely performed.

E. Hydroxyurea: Hydroxyurea is used to control high WCCs in conditions such as chronic myeloproliferative disorders but is not effective for hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic. She has suffered increasing tiredness over the past few months and finds it difficult to eat because of abdominal fullness and right upper quadrant pain. She has little past medical history of note, and her only medication is amlodipine for the treatment of hypertension. On examination, her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and pulse 85 bpm and regular. She looks pale. There is marked hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal palpation and peripheral lymphadenopathy.

Investigations;

InvestigationsResultsNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)42.2 × 109/L (smear cells seen on the film)4-11 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)145 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.5 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine110 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)122 IU/L5-30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)231 IU/L30-130 IU/L
Albumin32 g/l35-55 g/l
Bilirubin12 μmol/l2-17 μmol/L

Which of the following is the most useful next investigation in confirming the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Immunophenotyping: The most likely diagnosis is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), and immunophenotyping to look for circulating clonal B lymphocytes expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 and CD23, and an absence of FMC-7 staining to confirm the diagnosis, is an optimal next step. The differential pattern of receptor expression can also be used to differentiate from prolymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoma, as alternative differential diagnoses.

A. Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS): Abdominal USS will confirm hepatosplenomegaly and may reveal mesenteric lymph node enlargement, but it will not confirm this patient's underlying haematological diagnosis.

B. Bone marrow aspiration: Bone marrow biopsy can be useful with respect to determining the prognosis in CLL because the degree of abnormality seen in bone marrow architecture is linked to poorer outcomes. As the diagnosis can usually be obtained by immunophenotyping, bone marrow biopsy is not the next diagnostic approach here.

C. Chromosomal analysis: Chromosomal analysis may be useful with respect to determining prognosis, for instance patients carrying a deletion in chromosome 17 have a poorer outlook.

E. Lymph node biopsy: Lymph node biopsy is more usually carried out in patients with lymphoma, rather than those with leukaemia. In CLL, if significant enlargement of a single node or a group of nodes is seen, the node may be biopsied to rule out lymphomatous transformation.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe, unremitting epistaxis from both nostrils. The Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) Registrar successfully packs the nose. However, the patient complains of continuous post-nasal drip and has had several episodes of melaena. He has been suffering from prominent joint pains in the knees and hands for several months. There is no previous medical history of note, other than an uncomplicated hernia repair a year ago. Family history reveals nothing of significance. He is on no medication.

On examination, he has moderate synovitis of several proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal and large joints. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm and respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute. His skin is cool to touch. He is covered in large bruises.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)73 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.3 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)556 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)74 mm/hour1-20 mm/hour
Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) (does not correct in mixing study)75 seconds23.0-35.0 seconds
Prothrombin Test (PT)12 seconds10.6-14.9 seconds
Factor VIII activityReduced

What is the most appropriate therapy for this patient's bleeding?
questions.explanation:
E. Recombinant activated factor VII: Initially developed for use in patients with congenital haemophilia with alloantibody inhibitors, recombinant activated factor VII has been successfully used in patients with acquired haemophilia. It binds to the surface of activated platelets where it supports thrombin generation and bypasses the need for factor VIII.

C. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP): Given that FFP is a product derived from blood transfusion, it does contain factor VII. However, recombinant activated factor VII is much preferred, as it does not carry any risk of contamination.

A. Cryoprecipitate: Cryoprecipitate, derived from fresh frozen plasma (FFP), contains fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VIII, factor XIII and fibronectin, and is not likely to be effective here compared to activated factor VII.

B. Desmopressin: Desmopressin causes the release of von Willebrand factor from platelets, resulting in an increased level of factor VIII which is bound to it. Desmopressin may be used in patients with minor bleeding or before some elective procedures in patients with mild haemophilia A. Due to the severe nature of this bleed and the need for urgent treatment, it would not be appropriate to use desmopressin here since there would be a delay for factor VIII levels to rise in the body.

D. Recombinant factor VIII: This patient has an acquired factor VIII deficiency, probably associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Acquired haemophilia is more common in the elderly or during pregnancy, often in association with concurrent autoimmune disease or malignancy. It is due to an antibody to a coagulation factor, most commonly factor VIII, often referred to as an 'inhibitor'. Bleeding can be severe to the point that great care should be taken with cannula insertion, since compartment syndrome may ensue. Diagnosis is by performing mixing studies with patients and normal plasma - a simple factor deficiency will be corrected by mixing with normal plasma, but an acquired inhibitor will not correct with mixing. The inhibitor can then be measured by the Bethesda assay, which can be used to monitor response to treatment. Treatment with factor VIII is usually ineffective, as the inhibitor has rapid activity.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward from the Gastroenterology Clinic. She has ulcerative colitis which is usually quiescent. However, despite maximal mesalazine and prednisolone 60 mg daily, she is opening her bowels 8-10 times per day with bloody diarrhoea. On the ward, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and her heart rate is 92 bpm. Her temperature is 37.8°C. On examination, her abdomen is distended and tender, with sparse bowel sounds. Her right leg is also swollen.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/l115-155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.2 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)130 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)72 mg/L<10 mg/l
Sodium (Na+)139 mmol/l135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)3.8 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L
Abdominal X-ray (AXR)Dilated left-sided colon with evidence of mucosal oedema
Right leg venogramAbove-knee deep venous thrombosis

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her deep vein thrombosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Unfractionated heparin: Patients with an exacerbation of ulcerative colitis are at greatly increased risk of thromboembolic disease. This patient has an extensive right-sided deep vein thrombosis and is at significant risk of developing a pulmonary embolus. Heparinisation is the most appropriate intervention, which can be reversed in the event that surgery is required.

B. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH): Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is the usual initial drug of choice for a patient with deep vein thrombosis. Due to the state of the IBD flare, surgery is a significant possibility and LMWH would complicate this, given its half-life of 2-6 hours. Therefore, a shorter-acting drug, such as unfractionated heparin, is more appropriate.

A. Elastic stockings: Although stockings may be considered for prophylaxis, elastic stockings are not appropriate as a treatment for above-knee deep vein thrombosis.

C. Rivaroxaban: Rivaroxaban is a factor X inhibitor. Although it is useful as a long-term intervention for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism, it cannot be reversed easily if surgery is required.

D. Thrombectomy: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) flares are prothrombic. Although this patient has bloody diarrhoea, anticoagulation is indicated as long as the blood loss is not itself causing anaemia or haemodynamic instability (which it rarely does in IBD flares). Therefore, a surgical option is not necessary, as anticoagulation may be given, which is less invasive.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain. There is no known past medical history of note and he smokes 15-20 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.4 °C with a heart rate of 130 bpm and regular with a BP of 100/55 mmHg. There are coarse crackles at the right base, with a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 94% on 4 litres of oxygen delivered via nasal cannula. His lower limbs are examined, and a photograph is shown below:

Investigations:

InvestigationResultsNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)22.5 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)90 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Urea10.1 mmol/L1.8-7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)80 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
Fibrinogen1.2 g/l1.9-8.0 g/l
D-dimer7500 ng/ml<500 ng/ml
C-reactive protein (CRP)99 mg/L< 10 mg/l

What forms part of the immediate management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
B. Fresh frozen plasma: This patient has a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), given the presentation of sepsis of a likely respiratory origin. This patient has a CURB-65 score of 3 (respiratory rate over 30 breaths per minute, diastolic BP below 60 mmHg and urea over 7 mmol/l). A high CURB-65 score is associated with high mortality and an increased likelihood of complications such as DIC. DIC is an acquired syndrome characterised by dysregulation of the coagulation system leading to the formation of thrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors that, in turn, leads to bleeding. Laboratory markers of DIC include elevated fibrin degradation products (D-dimer). Other markers include a prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial prothrombin time and decreased fibrinogen and platelet count. Treatment of DIC includes finding and treating the underlying cause, which, in this case is with intravenous antibiotics. In addition to this, fresh frozen plasma is used in the immediate management of this patient. It is the preferred agent for replacing coagulation factors and is recommended as the first-line in current guidelines.

A. Cryoprecipitate: Cryoprecipitate is a second-line agent used in the treatment of DIC, particularly when there is a significant reduction in fibrinogen levels (below 1 g/l). Given that the fibrinogen levels are above 1 g/L and fresh frozen plasma is available, cryoprecipitate is the incorrect answer.

C. IV immunoglobulin: Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenia when there is associated bleeding or a high risk of bleeding, for example, in the preoperative setting. Although this patient has thrombocytopenia, additional signs of sepsis and significantly raised D-dimer are more suggestive of DIC.

D. Low-molecular-weight heparin: Low-molecular-weight heparin is used in the prophylaxis and management of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Although this patient has a raised D-dimer which is commonly used in the investigation of VTE, the history and presentation are more in keeping with pneumonia. Additionally, the combination of the purpuric rash on the lower limbs, clinical features of sepsis and a raised D-dimer are much more likely in keeping with DIC over VTE.

E. Prednisolone: Similar to intravenous immunoglobulin, prednisolone is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenia. Prednisolone is the first-line management of immune thrombocytopenia and is also used for managing vasculitic diseases that present with a similar rash as this patient. However, the combination of thrombocytopenia, sepsis and a significantly raised D-dimer is more suggestive of DIC.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old Cypriot tourist is admitted to A&E with severe abdominal pain. Over the last few days he had been coughing up green sputum and had pleuritic chest pain. He was given ciprofloxacin for presumed infection. This morning he awoke with sharp, very painful abdominal pain, worst in the epigastric area. No other symptoms. He drinks socially and doesn't smoke.

On examination, he is jaundiced and in pain. His temperature is 39.5°C. pulse 120 bpm, BP 102/48 mmHg and his respirations are 20 breaths/min. His saturations on room air are 95%. Some crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base can be heard. His abdomen is generally tender on palpation but with no guarding. Chest X-ray shows shadowing at the right lung base; ECG shows sinus tachycardia.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)62 g/l135-175 g/l
White Cell Count (WCC)17.3 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)465 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)136 mmol/L135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.5 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)84 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
Urea4.5 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Glucose5.7 mmol/L3.5-5.5 mmol/l
Albumin38 g/l35-55 g/l
Bilirubin71 μmol/l2-17 μmol/l
Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)62 IU/L5-30 IU/L
Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)124 IU/L30-130 IU/L
Amylase45 U/L< 200 U/L
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)97 fl80-100 fl
Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)1256 IU/L100-190 IU/L
UrineUrobilinogen+

Blood film: Heinz bodies and bite cells noted.

What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. G6PD deficiency: G6PD deficiency is the commonest red blood cell enzyme defect. It is a condition that is X-linked recessive in inheritance and is commonly found in Mediterranean and African populations. It is often triggered by infections, certain drugs (including ciprofloxacin), certain foods (including broad beans) and, at times, there can be no identifiable trigger. When exposed to an oxidative crisis there is typically a rapid haemolysis. Patients are often noted as having anaemia, Heinz bodies on blood film (due to haemolysis), an elevated LDH and reduced haptoglobin levels. The mainstay of treatment is supportive measures. In chronic disease, it may be appropriate to consider a splenectomy.

B. Familial Mediterranean fever: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive disease that is more commonly found in Mediterranean populations. It is characterised by short, recurrent episodes of fever, arthritis, peritonitis and pleuritis. During an attack, patients can have raised inflammatory markers (WCC, ESR, CRP) and diagnosis can be made following DNA analysis looking specifically for the FMF gene. The mainstay of treatment is colchicine. Interferon-a and etanercept can be used as alternatives. NSAIDs and steroids can also be used to help arthralgia and myalgia.

C. Atypical pneumonia: Atypical pneumonia is possible in this patient, but this is only part of the picture and would not explain the patient's blood findings such as anaemia and raised LDH. In this patient, the pneumonia ± antibiotics triggered the crisis in this G6PD-deficient patient.

D. Acute intermittent porphyria: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant condition in which the patient has a deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. It is a condition that is very difficult to diagnosis, but patients often present with unexplained abdominal pain, neurological or psychiatric symptoms, dark-coloured urine and cardiac arrhythmias.

E. Acute pancreatitis: As with this patient, most patients with pancreatitis present with severe abdominal pain which is usually epigastric. However, they tend to have a raised amylase that is greater than three times the upper limit of normal. It is not typical to develop a severe anaemia or to have the X-ray findings and symptoms of a cough. For causes, remember the mnemonic I GET SMASHED (Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Malignancy, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcaemia or hypertriglycerides, ERCP & Drugs). The mainstay of treatment is supportive measures such as IV fluids, keeping the patient nil by mouth, analgesia and antibiotics, if appropriate. In severe cases, patients may need admission to ICU.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman is admitted with a large haematoma of the right arm after minimal trauma. She has noticed over the past few weeks increased bruising of the skin. The patient has recently completed a course of penicillin for a chest infection. She has a past history of psoriasis and hypertension.

Examination reveals multiple bruises and a large painful haematoma in the right upper arm. The venepuncture site displays prolonged bleeding.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)9.8 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)325 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
International normalised ratio (INR)1.0< 1.1
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)53 s (30-40); does not correct with the addition of normal plasma23.0-35.0 s

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Acquired factor VIII deficiency: Acquired factor VIII deficiency results from the development of antibodies against factor VIII, which prevent its action. This can occur in the elderly and is associated with malignancy, psoriasis, pemphigus and drugs (cephalosporins, penicillins). Patients develop bleeding tendencies and the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged (intrinsic pathway). The APTT doesn't correct/will only correct slightly with the addition of normal plasma. The Bethesda titre can quantify the inhibitor. There is a 20% mortality rate from acquired factor VIII deficiency.

D. Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome: APAS is associated with a prolonged APTT, although it results in a propensity towards thrombosis rather than increased risk of bleeding.

A. Von Willebrand's disease: Although Von Willebrand's disease is associated with prolongation of APTT in 50% of patients due to low levels of factor VIII, it corrects on mixing with normal plasma.

B. Haemophilia A: Although haemophilia A does lead to bleeding and is associated with prolongation of APTT, presentation for the first time at this stage would be very unusual, and correction with normal plasma would be expected.

C. Haemophilia B: Haemophilia B is associated with bleeding, although correction of clotting disorder on mixing with normal plasma would be expected.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with indigestion of seven weeks' duration. She has no ongoing medical problems and is otherwise asymptomatic. She is on no medication.

Examination is unremarkable. She undergoes gastro-oesophageal endoscopy which reveals gastritis. Stomach biopsies confirm the presence of a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma/marginal zone lymphoma) of low-grade type; Helicobacter pylori is not demonstrated on biopsy. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis reveals no additional disease, and a bone marrow trephine is unremarkable; the stomach wall is not clearly thickened.

What should be the next stage in this patient's management?
options: A. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP)
C. Non-invasive testing for H. pylori
questions.explanation:
C. Non-invasive testing for H. pylori: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma), also known as marginal zone lymphomas, are low-grade lymphomas, most often diagnosed in the stomach. They are peculiar in that they are often associated with chronic inflammation of one of the following types:
• in the stomach secondary to chronic H. pylori gastritis
• in the eyes secondary to Sjögren syndrome
• in the thyroid secondary to Hashimoto's thyroiditis
• in the intestine secondary to Crohn's or coeliac disease.
Treatment against H. pylori is safe and will cause regression in 90% of low-grade gastric MALTomas. Due to the importance of establishing H. pylori diagnosis, if the tumour biopsy is negative for H. pylori, it is appropriate to perform non-invasive testing such as stool antigen testing or urea breath test for H. pylori. In the event that non-invasive testing reveals a positive result, the patient should be managed with triple therapy in the first instance.

A. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP): This would not be appropriate for this patient as R-cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (including rituximab) is a treatment option for more advanced gastric lymphoma.

B. High-dose dexamethasone: High-dose dexamethasone may provide symptomatic improvement but is ineffective in treating H. pylori, the likely trigger for mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma) seen here.

D. Observation alone: Observation alone risks significant lymphoma progression, meaning that H. pylori eradication would then be, in all likelihood, ineffective.

E. Partial gastrectomy: Surgery is rarely employed in the treatment of gastric MALToma because it is usually not curative and results in significant operative morbidity.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of worsening abdominal pain. She also complains of fatigue and nausea. There is no past medical history of note. She is 34 weeks pregnant.

On examination, her blood pressure is 159/95 mmHg and her heart rate is 102 bpm and regular. Chest sounds are clear and her heart sounds are normal. She has mild pedal oedema. On abdominal examination, there is palpable right upper quadrant tenderness.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)90 g/L135-180 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.2 × 109/l4-11 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)80 × 109/L150-450 × 109/L
Creatinine (Cr)88 μmol/L55-120 μmol/L
Bilirubin66 μmol/l3-17 μmol/l
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)210 u/L30-40 u/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)99 u/l30-100 u/l
C-reactive protein (CRP)22 mg/L<5 mg/l

Blood film: numerous schistocytes.

What would be the most appropriate definitive treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
D. Urgent Caesarean section: This woman has evidence of pre-eclampsia. This includes a deteriorating blood picture decreased platelet count (PLT) and abnormal liver enzymes and hypertension. Nearly 10% of women with severe pre-eclampsia and 30-50% of women with eclampsia are affected by the syndrome of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low PLT (HELLP). The exact relationship between HELLP syndrome and pre-eclampsia is unknown. Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome develop hepatocellular necrosis and liver dysfunction. They also have an increased mortality rate, and one-third of women with pre-eclampsia develop disseminated intravascular coagulation. The best treatment for this woman would be for an urgent Caesarean section to deliver the baby. Mild hypertension in pregnancy has been managed with oral nifedipine or labetalol. In this case, intravenous hydralazine or labetalol may well be required for blood pressure reduction/control preoperatively.

B. Intravenous magnesium sulfate: Intravenous magnesium is used in the treatment of eclampsia. In contrast, this patient has symptoms of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low PLT (HELLP) syndrome, for which magnesium is not used.

A. Intravenous labetalol: Although this patient has evidence of hypertension and possibly the beginning of pre-eclampsia (pending urinalysis), intravenous labetalol is not a definitive treatment. Rather, urgent Caesarean section to deliver the baby and pathological placenta is the only definitive treatment.

C. Plasma exchange: Plasma exchange is indicated for patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Features of TTP include haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, fever, acute kidney injury and cerebral dysfunction. Pregnancy is a predisposing factor. However, the combination of hypertension and deranged liver function tests makes HELLP syndrome most likely, for which the treatment is urgent delivery of the baby and the placenta.

E. Ursodeoxycholic acid: Ursodeoxycholic acid is used in symptomatic relief of itching in pregnant patients with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents more commonly in the third trimester and is associated with pruritus and raised bilirubin levels. However, the presence of haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and hypertension makes HELLP syndrome more likely.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the Haematology Clinic with complaints of fatigue, easy bruising and recurrent nosebleeds over the past month. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications.

On examination, she appears pale, with scattered petechiae on her arms and legs. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly is noted.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)75 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)1.2 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)20 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)88 fl80-100 fl
Reticulocyte count0.2%0.5-2.5%
Bone marrow biopsyHypocellular marrow with decreased haematopoietic cells, no abnormal infiltrates

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Aplastic anaemia: Aplastic anaemia is characterised by pancytopenia, with a hypocellular bone marrow devoid of abnormal infiltrates. The patient's presentation with fatigue, easy bruising, recurrent nosebleeds and pancytopenia, with a hypocellular bone marrow, is consistent with this diagnosis.

A. Acute myeloid leukaemia: While acute myeloid leukaemia can cause pancytopenia, it typically presents with an elevated number of abnormal myeloblasts in the blood and bone marrow. This patient's bone marrow biopsy does not show any abnormal infiltrates, which makes leukaemia less likely.

B. Myelodysplastic syndrome: Myelodysplastic syndrome can present with pancytopenia and a hypocellular or hypercellular marrow, with dysplastic changes in haematopoietic cells. However, the bone marrow in aplastic anaemia is typically hypocellular without dysplasia, as seen in this patient.

C. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) generally causes isolated thrombocytopenia without affecting Hb levels or the WCC. The presence of pancytopenia in this patient rules out ITP as a likely diagnosis.

E. Megaloblastic anaemia: Megaloblastic anaemia, caused by deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folate, can result in pancytopenia but usually presents with a high MCV due to the presence of large, immature red cells. This patient's normal MCV makes this diagnosis unlikely.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old Greek woman with beta-thalassaemia major, and who has had several blood transfusions and uses desferrioxamine for prevention of iron overload, comes to the clinic with her sister who is 25 years old and wants to start a family. They want to discuss the mutation that is the basis of the 18-year old's underlying disease.

Which of the following is the basis of beta-thalassaemia major?
options: D. 1 alpha- and one beta-chain gene mutation
questions.explanation:
E. 2 beta-chain mutations: Beta-thalassaemia major is due to mutations in the genes coding for each of the beta-globin chains. This results in grossly ineffective erythropoiesis and severe hypochromic microcytic anaemia with iron overload. The profound anaemia is associated with erythroid hyperplasia and extramedullary haemopoiesis. Given that her parents were unaffected by thalassaemia major but must have suffered from the thalassaemia trait, the 25-year-old sister has a 66% chance of having the thalassaemia trait, (she is symptomless, meaning that she must either be normal or carry a mutation for 1 of the 2 beta-globin genes). She should be advised to have haemoglobin electrophoresis prior to beginning a family with her new partner.

D. 1 alpha- and one beta-chain gene mutation: Mixed alpha- and beta-thalassaemia is said to carry a milder clinical course than thalassaemia major.

A. 1 alpha-chain gene mutation: One alpha-chain mutation leads to so-called silent alpha-thalassaemia, which is asymptomatic.

B. 1 beta-chain gene mutation: This leads to beta-thalassaemia trait, which is the likely diagnosis in the 25-year-old sibling of the patient with thalassaemia major.

C. 2 alpha-chain gene mutations: Two alpha-chain mutations lead to alpha-thalassaemia trait microcytic anaemia, which is usually asymptomatic.

questions.question:
A 74-year-old patient presents to the GP with headache, dizziness, vertigo, vague abdominal pain and general lethargy. He has previously been fit and well, with mild hypertension as his only significant past medical history.

On examination his BP is 155/95 mmHg and he has a ruddy complexion.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin179 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)19.5 × 109/L4-11 × 109/L
Platelets450 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)141 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.9 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine145 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
Haematocrit0.56

You suspect primary polycythaemia. Which of the following investigations is most likely to provide a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. JAK-2 mutation testing: JAK-2 mutation testing is widely available, with the V617F mutation being found in approximately 96% of patients with primary polycythaemia. The protein is a signalling protein within the JAK-STAT pathway, which drives production of red blood cells.

C. Arterial blood gas estimation: Absence of hypoxia makes secondary polycythaemia less likely, although in conditions such as obesity hypoventilation syndrome, where hypoxia is more marked at night, hypoxia may be missed in the clinic.

A. LDH levels: Although LDH levels are elevated in the presence of haematological malignancy, they are non-specific so could not be used to confirm a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia here.

D. Uric acid levels: Uric acid levels are raised in patients with primary polycythaemia due to increased red blood cell turnover, although elevated uric acid may also be seen due to a number of other causes.

E. C282Y mutation testing: C282Y mutation testing is most useful as a screening test for hereditary haemochromatosis.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male nurse presents with prolonged bleeding after a routine dental extraction. It is two days since the procedure, and the bleeding has been continuous: he has noticed black stools on three separate occasions.

Past medical history includes a postoperative haemorrhage following tonsillectomy, that required a blood transfusion. He has one brother who is well and believes a cousin may have died of bleeding during childbirth.

On examination, he is pale but well perfused. Rectal examination confirms melaena.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)81 g/l135-175 g/l
Prothrombin Test (PT)28 s10.6-14.9 s
Partial Thromboplastin Time (PTT)33 s23.0-35.0 s
Fibrinogen230 mg/dl125-300 mg/dl

Mixing studies with 50:50 test normal plasma shows complete correction of PT.

What diagnosis should be considered at this stage pending further investigation?
questions.explanation:
D. Inherited Factor VII deficiency: Factor VII is the only factor unique to the prothrombin time (PT), and deficiency of Factor VII therefore gives a prolonged PT and normal APTT. Deficiencies of II, V and X will prolong both activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) and PT. Deficiencies of XII, XI, IX and VIII will prolong APTT alone. When an abnormality is detected in the PT/APTT, the studies are repeated with a 50:50 mix of test and normal plasma: straightforward factor deficiencies will correct with mixing, but inhibitors (most commonly lupus anticoagulant) do not correct.

B. Self-dosing with warfarin: Given that other family members have been affected by a clotting disorder, and PT is prolonged without prolongation of APTT. this effectively rules out warfarin self-dosing as the underlying cause.

A. Inherited Factor IX deficiency: Factor IX deficiency results in prolongation of APTT, and would correct with normal plasma mixing.

C. Acquired Factor IX deficiency: Acquired Factor IX deficiency would prolong the APTT and would not correct with normal plasma.

E. Acquired Factor VII deficiency: Acquired Factor VII deficiency due to an inhibitor antibody would not correct with normal plasma.

questions.question:
You are asked to counsel a married couple expecting a baby. They are both fit and well, with no previous medical history. They both originate from South East Asia, and have no family history of birth abnormalities. There are no abnormalities on examination.

Investigations reveal the following:

MALE

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)117 g/l135-175 g/l
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)70 fl76-98 fl
Mean cell haemoglobin (MCНЬ)19 pg27-32 pg
Red cell count5.6 × 1012/L4.7-6.9 × 1012/L
Haemoglobin electrophoresisnormal

FEMALE

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)101 g/l115-155 g/l
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)68 fl76-98 fl
Mean cell haemoglobin (MCHЬ)18 pg27-32 pg
Red cell count6.0 × 1012/L4.7-6.9 × 1012/l
Haemoglobin electrophoresisnormal

What condition is the fetus at risk from developing?
questions.explanation:
C. Hydrops fetalis: Both patients come from an area endemic for a-thalassaemia, and appear to be carriers, with normal red blood cell counts and hypochromia/microcytosis. It's important to remember that in a-thalassaemia the Hb electrophoresis is usually normal. Hydrops fetalis is associated with homozygous alpha-thalassaemia, thus driving the correct answer.

B. Thalassaemia intermedia: The terms thalassaemia minor, intermedia and major do not pertain to a- or β-thalassaemia rather they describe whether the patient is asymptomatic (minor), transfusion dependent (major) or in between (intermedia). Loss of a single a chain (aa/-a) is common (30% in Africa); loss of two a chains (aa/--) is less common, and co-inheritance can lead to hydrops fetalis (--/--), where no a chains are produced, and haemoglobin (Hb) Barts is produced (a gamma-4 tetramer). Loss of three alpha chains (a-/--) leads to haemoglobin H (HbH) disease (HbH is composed of beta-4 tetramers), usually with a thalassaemia intermedia phenotype.

A. B-Thalassaemia trait: Patients with β-thalassaemia trait nearly always have a raised haemoglobin A2 and fetal haemoglobin on haemoglobin electrophoresis (although normal A2 variants do exist). The fact that both parents have normal haemoglobin electrophoresis means there is effectively very low/no significant risk of the fetus developing beta-thalassaemia trait.

D. B-Thalassaemia major: β-Thalassaemia trait in the parents has effectively been ruled out by the normal haemoglobin electrophoresis, and therefore β-thalassaemia won't occur in the fetus in this case.

E. Homozygous haemoglobin E: Haemoglobin-E is associated with mild β-thalassaemia which presents in the first few months of life, and isn't usually a cause of fetal loss.

questions.question:
