You are asked to see a 20-year-old man with a temperature of 39°C. He is an in-patient receiving an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. He was diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia three months previously and was treated with imatinib mesylate, which brought about a rapid haematological and cytogenetic remission.

He received myeloablative conditioning with total body irradiation and cyclophosphamide 10 days previously and received stem cells collected from his brother, with whom he is fully HLA (human leukocyte antigen) compatible. He first became febrile five days ago and has received ceftazidime (changed to meropenem after 48 h) and vancomycin intravenously.

Examination shows an unwell young man; pulse 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, heart sounds normal; capillary refill < 2 s; respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, crackles in the right mid-zone; abdomen normal. Urine output is above 30 ml/h and has been negative to date.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)93 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)0.2 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)12 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Blood culturesNegative at 48 hour
Urine culturesNegative at 48 hour
Chest X-ray (CXR)Right middle lobe patchy consolidation

What is the most appropriate management?
options: A. Add in metronidazole for anaerobic cover
B. Change vancomycin to linezolid to cover vancomycin resistant enterococcus
C. Add in acyclovir 10 mg/kg to cover systemic herpes infection
D. Add in liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg to cover invasive aspergillosis
E. Add in intravenous fluconazole 400 mg daily to cover invasive candidiasis
questions.explanation:
D. Add in liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg to cover invasive aspergillosis: The gravest concern is that the fevers are due to invasive aspergillosis (IA) or related fungal infection. Systemic herpes infection or candidiasis are both possible, but less likely. Diagnosing IA is difficult; computed tomography of the chest is useful at identifying lesions, but is not completely sensitive or specific. Bronchoscopy with lavage suffers from the same limitations, and invasive procedures are discouraged in neutropenic patients. Various serological assays have been trialled, including using the polymerase chain reaction to detect early invasive disease. IA can only be confidently diagnosed by the finding of characteristic hyphae on a biopsy specimen, but for obvious reasons this is rarely available. Vorconazole is the treatment of choice followed by posaconazole. Amphoteracin is used if neither of these agents is effective. Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin can be used if first-line agents are either ineffective or not tolerated. Any immunosuppressive drugs may be reduced, or granulocyte-stimulating colony factor can be used to rectify neutropenia whilst a patient is unwell

A. Add in metronidazole for anaerobic cover: The patient has been well treated for neutropenic sepsis and meropenem will provide reasonable anaerobic cover, so metronidazole is not required.

B. Change vancomycin to linezolid to cover vancomycin resistant enterococcus: VRE would only be considered at this point if there was microbiological evidence.

C. Add in acyclovir 10 mg/kg to cover systemic herpes infection: Although systemic herpes infection is possible, it is less likely than other infections such as fungal infections and, as such, would not be the next step in treatment.

E. Add in intravenous fluconazole 400 mg daily to cover invasive candidiasis: Invasive candidiasis should be a consideration but is less likely to be the cause of the ongoing symptoms than invasive aspergillosis and treatment of candidiasis would, therefore, not be the next step.

questions.question:
A 69-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-month history of progressive lethargy and malaise. He also complains of persistent headaches, dizziness and blurred vision for the last three months. His past medical history includes hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

On examination, he appears pale and very slim. His heart sounds are normal and there is equal air entry bilaterally, with minimal expiratory wheeze. On abdominal examination, there is palpable hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)88 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.5 × 109/L4-11 × 109/L
Mean cell volume (MCV)75 fl70-90 fl
Platelets350 × 109/L150-450 × 109/l
Sodium (Na+)136 mmol/L135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)3.6 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine88 mmol/l50-120mmol/L
Calcium2.4 mmol/L2.1-2.6 mmol/L
Phosphate1.2 mmol/L0.8-1.4 mmol/L

Serum electrophoresis shows paraproteinaemia, which is predominantly immunoglobulin M (IgM) (5 g/l).

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS)
questions.explanation:
E. Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia: This patient has a diagnosis of Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia, a lymphoplasmacytoid malignancy associated with increased monoclonal production of the IgM paraprotein. Symptoms and signs include lethargy. weight loss, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Increased levels of paraproteins increase plasma viscosity, causing hyperviscosity syndrome that often presents as headache, dizziness and blurred vision. The condition is more often seen in older men, such as what is seen in this patient.

D. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes that causes painless lymphadenopathy. in addition to systemic symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fever. Hepatosplenomegaly is an extranodal sign. However, the presence of raised paraprotein levels is not typical of Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

A. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a malignancy of the lymphoid lineage of cells (most commonly B cells). It is the most common malignancy in adults and is often detected incidentally. Symptoms that may be present include lethargy, lymphadenopathy, weight loss and symptoms of hyperviscosity syndrome as WCC increases. However, this patient has a raised paraprotein level with a normal WCC, making CLL unlikely.

B. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS): Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS) is a benign condition that is caused by raised monoclonal paraproteinaemia without the presence of symptoms. Given that this patient has symptomatic anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and hyperviscosity syndrome, MGUS is an unlikely diagnosis.

C. Multiple myeloma: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of bone marrow plasma cells that causes paraproteinaemia (typically immunoglobulin G (IgG) or immunoglobulin A (IgA)) and symptoms and signs of anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia and bone disease such as pathological fractures. Multiple myeloma presents between 60 and 70 years of age and is an important differential diagnosis to have for this clinical scenario. However, the lack of renal impairment and bone disease, along with isolated monoclonal gammopathy of IgM paraprotein, makes Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia much more likely.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman who underwent right hemicolectomy opted to receive a designated blood transfusion from her daughter, who is the same blood group. Whilst on the ward undergoing the first unit of blood she began to complain of extreme shortness of breath. Her blood pressure was markedly reduced, at 90/50 mmHg. On examination there were inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields. Dipstick of her urine was negative for haematuria.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this transfusion reaction?
options: C. Granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood
D. Granulocyte antibodies in the recipient blood
E. Cytokines in the donor blood
questions.explanation:
C. Granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood: Transfusion-related lung injury or TRALI is thought to be related to anti-HLA or anti-granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood. Despite the fact that the donor and recipient are matched, the possibility of anti-granulocyte antibodies cannot be excluded. It is postulated that TRALI is seen more often in multiparous women who donate blood, because of the generation of antibodies to HLA antigens through multiple exposures to fetal blood. Lung symptoms are often difficult to distinguish from ARDS, and management of TRALI is consistent with the management of ARDS itself.

D. Granulocyte antibodies in the recipient blood: It is antibodies in the donor blood against neutrophils in the recipient that may have undergone priming due to an acute respiratory illness, which drive the presentation here.

A. ABO incompatibility: ABO incompatibility is associated with an acute deterioration characterised by hypotension, tachycardia, haemolysis and symptoms similar to anaphylaxis, although the reaction isn't mediated by IgE. It carries a mortality of up to 10%.

B. Rhesus incompatibility: Rhesus incompatibility presents with a similar picture to ABO incompatibility, but symptoms are generally less severe.

E. Cytokines in the donor blood: Cytokines in donor blood are associated with febrile transfusion reactions. There are normally no other sequelae apart from an increase in body temperature and mild tachycardia.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of abdominal distension, lower limb swelling and yellowish discolouration of his eyes for the past three months. The patient also complains of difficulty concentrating and easy fatiguability over this period and feels he has put on a lot of weight due to generalised swelling. He has had a decreased urine output for the past three weeks and there are days when he passes only about 50 ml of urine.

The peripheral smear done is shown below:

Which of the following has caused the red blood cell (RBC) abnormality in this patient?
questions.explanation:
C. Liver dysfunction: The RBC abnormality in the given peripheral smear is macrocytosis. Liver disease is a known cause of macrocytosis. This patient's presentation with features of volume overload and jaundice is typical of chronic liver disease. The decreased renal output in this patient may signify hepatorenal syndrome, rather than a primary renal abnormality.

D. Renal dysfunction: Renal dysfunction has not been known to cause macrocytosis. However, chronic kidney disease may be associated with folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiencies, which may cause macrocytosis. In addition, patients on long-term haemodialysis may also have macrocytosis. However, in this patient, the decreased urine output is likely due to hepatorenal syndrome.

A. Folate deficiency: Although folate deficiency can cause macrocytosis, liver dysfunction is more likely to be the cause in this patient.

B. Hypothyroidism: Although hypothyroidism can cause macrocytosis, it is unlikely to be the cause in this patient.

E. Vitamin B12 deficiency: Although vitamin B12 deficiency can cause macrocytosis, liver dysfunction is more likely to be the cause in this patient.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman is bought to her GP by her carer who has become concerned after noticing that the patient's gums have progressively become more prominent over the last few months. She tried to take the patient to the dentist but no NHS dental appointments were available. The patient lives in a home since she has learning difficulties. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for three infections in the last 6 weeks. The carer has also noticed that recently the patient has become increasingly fatigued by even the lightest of activities and is commonly short of breath on exertion. She is not currently on any medications but has taken various courses of antibiotics recently.

On examination, she is noted to be anaemic and has multiple bruises over her body. She has hypertrophic bleeding gums and, on auscultation of the heart, she is found to have a flow murmur. She has mild splenomegaly on palpation of her abdomen. Routine blood tests were requested and confirmed the presence of anaemia, a raised white cell count, low neutrophil count and thrombocytopenia. A blood film shows increased numbers of blast cells and the presence of Auer rods.

Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML): Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a malignant disease of the bone marrow in which the blast cells derived from the myeloid marrow elements undergo a neoplastic proliferation. AML is distinguished by the presence of >20% blasts in the blood and/or bone marrow. It is more common in men and the prevalence increases with age, but it can affect all age groups. It is, however, becoming more common as a long-term complication of chemotherapy. Symptoms are usually related to marrow failure (anaemia, infections, bleeding) and/or organ infiltration with leukaemic cells (bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, gum hypertrophy, proptosis), but patients can also have constitutional symptoms (weakness, fever, lethargy).

C. Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): CML is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by the proliferation of the precursors for white blood cells, but these precursors retain the ability to differentiate. Symptoms tend to be chronic and the blood profile shows an increased (++) white cell count, with a low or normal haemoglobin and a variable platelet count.

B. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL): AML is differentiated from ALL by the presence of Auer rods, which are eosinophilic needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions found in blast cells and that are pathognomonic of AML.

D. Chronic lymphoid leukaemia (CLL): The most noteworthy laboratory abnormality found in CLL is lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood and bone marrow. Although the absolute blood lymphocyte threshold for diagnosing CLL has been placed at >5000/microl (5 × 109/l) B lymphocytes, a significant proportion of patients presents with counts as high as 100,000/microl (100 × 109/L) The peripheral blood smear of patients with CLL demonstrates a lymphocytosis. The leukemic cells are typically small, mature-appearing lymphocytes with a dense nucleus, partially aggregated (clumped) chromatin and lacking discernible nucleoli. There is a narrow border of clear to slightly basophilic cytoplasm. The blood film in this scenario is not that of CLL.

E. Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML): CMML is characterised by a progressive cytopenia in the presence of a hypercellular bone marrow and usually involves all three cell lines (myeloid/monocyte, erythroid, megakaryocyte).

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman presents with back pain over the past several months. She has hypertension which is currently controlled on two oral agents and a long history of osteoarthritis affecting her hips and her back.

On examination, she looks relatively well, has a normal blood pressure (BP) of 142/82 mmHg and there are no significant findings on physical examination.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.8 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)201 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)139 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)5.4 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 μmol/L50-120 μmol/l
Bone marrow8% plasma cells
MM-protein found on electrophoresis22 g/l

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS)
questions.explanation:
A. Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS): According to guidelines, this patient seems likely to have MGUS. The criteria for diagnosis of MGUS include an M-protein level of <30 g/l, <10% plasma cells on bone marrow investigation and no end organ damage associated with myeloma. There should also be no evidence of amyloidosis.

E. Myelodysplasia: Unexplained macrocytic anaemia may predate the diagnosis of myelodysplasia by months or years, and neutropenia and low platelets are also seen. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are very uncommonly seen in patients with myelodysplasia.

B. Multiple myeloma: The fact that the percentage of plasma cells in bone marrow is less than 10% effectively rules out multiple myeloma here.

C. Asymptomatic myeloma: Where there is no end organ damage and more than 10% of the bone marrow contains plasma cells, or M-protein is >30 g/l, then this is deemed asymptomatic myeloma.

D. Myelofibrosis: Myelofibrosis is associated with anaemia, with tear-drop red cells, a leuko-erythroblastic blood picture and splenomegaly, features not seen here.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a massively swollen left leg. She has most recently been laid up in bed with an episode of influenza, and puts her leg problem down to a lack of movement. Past medical history of note includes 4 miscarriages which all occurred between the 10th and the 16th week of pregnancy. She stopped taking the oral contraceptive pill in her twenties because of migraine.

Examination reveals a massively swollen left leg, and USS confirms an extensive deep vein thrombosis extending into the femoral vein. APTT is prolonged at 45.8 s, and does not correct on mixing with normal plasma.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome: The answer is Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, (APAS) - APAS is associated with presence of the lupus anti-coagulant, (failure of APTT to correct with normal plasma), and increased risk of both venous thrombosis and miscarriage. As such the clinical picture here fits best with APAS. This patient is likely to require life long anti-coagulation.

D. Inherited factor VIII deficiency: Inherited factor VIII deficiency, is incorrect, this is associated with increased risk of bleeding and a prolonged APTT which corrects on mixing with normal plasma.

A. Acquired factor VIII deficiency: Acquired factor VIII deficiency, is incorrect because although it is associated with prolonged APTT that fails to correct, it is associated with increased risk of bleeding.

C. Factor V Leiden mutation: Factor V Leiden mutation, is incorrect, it is associated with increased risk of thrombosis, although the APTT is in the normal range, ruling it out here.

E. Von Willebrand's disease: Von Willebrand's disease, is incorrect, this is associated with increased risk of bleeding and a prolonged APTT and is therefore not the likely cause of this patient's symptoms.

questions.question:
This is the family tree of a family affected with haemophilia A (males denoted by squares, females denoted by circles).

What are the chances of 'M' being affected?
questions.explanation:
B. 1 in 2: Haemophilia A is a sex-linked inherited disease in humans. Males are hemizygous and receive their only X chromosome from their mother. Females are heterozygous and receive one X chromosome from each parent. Consequently, if a male has an affected X chromosome, he will be affected by an X-linked disease. In the above family tree, the daughter of the affected individual will receive the diseased X chromosome from her father and a normal X chromosome from her mother, so that she is a carrier of the disease. Her son, in turn, will have a 1 in 2 chance of receiving the diseased chromosome from his carrier mother, so the chance of him being affected with haemophilia A is 1 in 2.

C. 1 in 3: 1 in 3 is the chance of the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder being normal (i.e. not a carrier), if they are proven not to suffer from the disease.

A. 1 in 1: This patient's mother will carry the haemophilia gene on one of her X-chromosomes, but the other is normal. This means there is a 50% chance of male offspring inheriting haemophilia.

D. 1 in 4: 1 in 4 is the chance of the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder either being normal or suffering from the disease in question.

E. 1 in 6: 1 in 6 doesn't fit with a pattern of Mendelian inheritance.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old South African man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department. He is confused, but you can get a history from his wife. He is on holiday in the UK for a week. He is normally in good health and was well when he arrived in the UK. The only past history of note is an admission some 3 years earlier with acute lower abdominal pain and agitation. He is on no regular medications but took some over-the-counter antihistamines yesterday for hay fever. Since then, he has been complaining of a weak arm, vomiting and abdominal pain. When he became confused, his wife became concerned and brought him to Accident and Emergency.

On examination, he is confused and hallucinating. He has bilateral wrist drop. Otherwise, examination of his peripheral nervous system and cranial nerves is normal. Pulse is 120/min and regular, and his BP is 175/100 mmHg. Examination of his chest is also normal. Examination of his abdomen reveals diffuse tenderness.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Sodium (Na+)120 mmol/L135-145 mmoU
Potassium (K+)4.3 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Urea6.0 mmol/l2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)120 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L

He is given a bolus of IV glucose, what other measure would you take next?
options: B. Alcohol withdrawal regime of chlordiazepoxide
questions.explanation:
A. IV haem arginate: This describes an attack of acute intermittent porphyria. The diagnosis requires demonstration of increased urinary excretion of the haem precursor, porphobilinogen (PBG), in the urine. Urine characteristically turns red on standing. All attacks of porphyria increase the activity of hepatic 5-aminolevulinate (ALA) synthase, which can be measured in serum. The relation between these biochemical abnormalities and the neuronal dysfunction that underlies all the features of an acute attack is uncertain. Two procedures have been shown to decrease the activity of ALA synthase in animals - carbohydrate loading and parenteral infusion of haem arginate. Consequently, these two procedures are the mainstay of the treatment along with opiate analgesia. Provoking medication, such as the antihistamines in this case, should be withdrawn.

C. Intravenous thiamine: We aren't given a significant alcohol consumption history as part of the scenario, and the previous episode 3 years ago of abdominal pain fits with intermittent porphyria, and thus thiamine is not likely to be effective here.

B. Alcohol withdrawal regime of chlordiazepoxide: Chlordiazepoxide is a benzodiazepine type sedative, but it won't manage the underlying cause of this patient's agitation, an acute episode of porphyria.

D. IV cyclizine: Cyclizine is an anti-emetic with some antihistamine activity; reports about its safety conflict with respect to use in porphyria, with some case reports suggesting it can be used and others raising the possibility that it can precipitate porphyria episodes.

E. Abdominal CT: The symptoms of pseudo-obstruction with hypertension and hyponatraemia are most consistent with acute intermittent porphyria; the abdominal CT is therefore most likely to be normal.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner complaining of increasing bruising. She has undergone a bone marrow transplant from a human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched family member for previous acute myeloid leukaemia. On examination, she has a number of areas of bruising and looks pale. Her blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)3.9 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)6.0 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na )141 mmol/L135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.9 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)121 μmol/l50-120 μmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate form of platelets to use for transfusion?
questions.explanation:
C. Gamma-irradiated: Patients who have undergone bone marrow transplantation are at increased risk of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease because of lymphocytes within the donor material. Gamma-irradiated blood products are generally recommended for patients undergoing human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched transfusions and those with an inherited immune system disorder, an acquired immune disorder such as Hodgkin's disease or post-bone marrow transplantation. Irradiation minimises the chances of surviving leukocytes being found within donated platelets.

B. Family-donated: Family-donated platelets are still associated with an increased risk of graft-versus-host disease and should therefore be avoided here.

A. Beta-irradiated: Beta-irradiation is a technique used to sterilise pharmaceutical packaging products and medical devices. It is gamma-irradiation that is used to sterilise transfusions.

D. human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched: Usually, HLA-matched platelets are considered for patients who have become refractory to platelet transfusions because of the presence of anti-HLA antibodies.

E. Washed: Platelet washing is designed to remove about 99% of plasma. It does, however, result in decreased quality of platelet function, is labour- and time-intensive and can result in delays to transfusion.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old Asian man presents to the Pre-clerking Clinic prior to his laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones. He has a history of hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg, but no other past medical history of note.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)104 g/l135-175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.5 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)195 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)139 mmol/L135-145 mmol/L
Potassium (K+)4.5 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)105 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)60 fl80-100 fl
Ferritin300 μ mol/L24-355 μmol/l
Upper Gl endoscopyNormal
TIBCNormal

Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the underlying cause of his anaemia?
questions.explanation:
D. Haemoglobin electrophoresis: This man has asymptomatic microcytic anaemia and he is of Asian ethnic origin. His upper Gl endoscopy is normal, as is his ferritin, which reduces the possibility of this being iron deficiency anaemia. The most likely cause is beta-thalassaemia trait, the diagnosis of which is best confirmed with haemoglobin electrophoresis. Patients with thalassaemia trait do not usually require any intervention. Bearing in mind that his ferritin of 300 is within the normal range, his anaemia will not be responsive to iron supplementation. Chelation therapy is only required in patients with thalassaemia major. Blood loss associated with laparoscopic cholescystectomy is likely to be relatively minor, and so blood transfusion would not be required prior to surgery.

A. Colonoscopy: This would be the appropriate investigation for iron deficiency anaemia after a normal gastroscopy.

B. Mesenteric angiography: This would be the investigation of choice in cases of unexplained blood loss or unidentifiable source (normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy), and in persistent iron deficiency anaemia.

C. Transferrin: High transferrin levels are seen in iron deficiency anaemia, with subsequent decrease of the transferrin saturation and increase in TIBC (total iron-binding capacity).

E. Bone marrow aspirate: This is performed for the diagnosis of lympho- or myeloproliferative disorders.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with myelodysplasia complains of breathlessness on exertion. He was diagnosed with myelodysplasia three years ago and since then has been on two units of blood every three weeks to maintain his haemoglobin above 100 g/l. He has noticed over the last three months increasing exertional breathlessness despite maintaining his haemoglobin above 10.

Examination shows a slim man with greyish skin colour. His heart rate is 90 bpm, sinus rhythm. Heart sounds are normal. Jugular venous pressure is not raised. The cardiac apex is palpable at the anterior axillary line. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest and the abdominal examination is normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)113 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)1.3 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)23 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Neutrophils0.3 × 109/L2.5-7.58 × 109/L
Glucose12.4 mmol/L3.5-5.5 mmol/L

What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: A. Increase the transfusion program to maintain haemoglobin above 120 g/l
B. Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise the haemoglobin to 120 g/l
C. Start venesection program to reduce ferritin to less than 1000
D. Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine
E. Commence hydroxyurea or similar cytotoxic to treat myelodysplasia
questions.explanation:
D. Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine: This patient has early signs of iron overload secondary to chronic blood transfusion - grey skin, early heart failure and diabetes. There are limited options for intervention, and given the transfusion needs of this patient with iron overload, desferrioxamine is the most appropriate choice. It needs to be given for 8-12 h per day for 5-7 days per week and is thus a major undertaking for the patient. Side effects of therapy are common and include high-frequency deafness and retinopathy.

E. Commence hydroxyurea or similar cytotoxic to treat myelodysplasia: Hydroxyurea won't reduce transfusion requirements or iron overload in the short term, and thus intervention with an iron chelator is the preferred choice here.

A. Increase the transfusion program to maintain haemoglobin above 120 g/l: This runs the risk of further worsening iron overload and won't improve symptoms of cardiac failure.

B. Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise the haemoglobin to 120 g/L: Commencing erythropoietin to reduce the transfusion requirement is an attractive option, but is only likely to work in patients with low transfusion requirements (<1 unit per month) and does not address the underlying problem of iron overload.

C. Start venesection program to reduce ferritin to less than 1000: Although this would impact on iron overload, it would worsen anaemia and defeat the object of regular transfusions.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman who works at a local day nursery is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe headache and weakness affecting the left-hand side of her face. She has been unwell for the past few days with headaches, anorexia and diarrhoea. Apparently, she has eaten the same food as a number of children at the nursery who have fallen ill with diarrhoea - two of whom are in the local hospital with kidney disease.

On examination, her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There is evidence of a purpuric rash and petechial haemorrhages. Abdomen is soft and generally tender, and she has active bowel sounds. You confirm left upper motor neurone 7th nerve palsy.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)99 g/l (schistocytes on blood film)135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)12.1 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)32 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/L135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)5.2 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)141 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)950 u/l140-280 u/l
UrineBlood ++ protein ++

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
D. Plasma exchange: The history and blood picture seen here is consistent with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). TTP is a rare blood disorder that features extensive microscopic clots that form in the small blood vessels throughout the body causing damage to the kidneys, heart and brain. Most cases of TTP arise from autoantibody-mediated inhibition of the enzyme ADAMTS13, a metalloprotease responsible for cleaving large multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF) into smaller units. The increase in circulating multimers of vWF increases platelet adhesion to areas of endothelial injury, particularly at arteriole-capillary junctions. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome has a similar pathogenic process, although it presents with predominant renal impairment rather than neurological dysfunction. Plasma exchange is the initial therapy of choice, which has been associated with a reduction in mortality rate to less than 25% since its introduction.

B. Intravenous immunoglobulin: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is a potential interim solution until plasma exchange is available, but there is no role for intravenous immunoglobulin therapy.

A. Ciprofloxacin: Ciprofloxacin has no role to play in the treatment of TTP. Ciprofloxacin may be useful in infection; however, there is no indication of infection in this scenario.

C. Intravenous methylprednisolone: There is no evidence that corticosteroids or antibiotics have any benefit in the management of TTP. Current therapy is based on support and plasmapheresis to reduce circulating antibodies against ADAMTS13 and replenish blood levels of the enzyme. Methylprednisolone will not reduce the levels of the circulating antibodies.

E. Platelet transfusion: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage, although platelets are consumed and there is typically a thrombocytopenia in TTP. The diagnostic criteria for TTP includes fevers, change in mental status, a low platelet count, decreased renal function and anaemia due to shearing by blood clots in the small blood vessels (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia).

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman presents with fatigue and confusion that has come on gradually over several weeks. She is a retired secondary school teacher who was still tutoring on a part-time basis until 3 months ago but has recently become reliant on family and neighbours for basic self-care. She has no previous medical history of note and is taking only antacids for occasional dyspepsia.

On examination, she is obese, with a blood pressure of 175/100 mmHg. She is disorientated; tone, power and reflexes are all within normal limits. Plantar responses are downgoing. Fundoscopy shows prominent retinal veins, but is otherwise normal. There are bi-basal crackles at both bases.

Blood tests are shown below:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.3 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)120 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Urea10.3 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/L
Bilirubin21 μmol/L1-22 μmol/L
Albumin29 g/l35-55 g/l
Total protein113 g/l60-83 g/l
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)95 mm/h1-20 mm/h
Corrected calcium (Ca2+)2.3 mmol/L2.2-2.7 mmol/L

What test is most likely to help establish the cause of confusion?
options: B. Urine for Bence Jones protein
questions.explanation:
C. Serum protein electrophoresis: The question asks for the test most likely to confirm the cause of the confusion. Myeloma or Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia leading to clinically significant hyperviscosity are the most likely cause here. Serum immunoglobulins do not confirm the presence of a paraprotein, whereas serum protein electrophoresis will. This is because a number of inflammatory conditions may result in a global increase in immunoglobulins. If a paraprotein is found, a bone marrow trephine can help make a tissue diagnosis of an associated myeloma [in the case of immunoglobulin G (IgG)/immunoglobulin A (IgA) paraproteins or lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma [in the case of immunoglobulin M (IgM) paraprotein] and help to differentiate between Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia and myeloma, but this test will not directly help explain the patient's confusion. Great care should be exercised before patients with hyperviscosity are transfused, as any further increase in viscosity may precipitate a cerebral event. Treatment is with chemotherapy targeted to the underlying condition and, where transfusion is urgently required, plasmapheresis first.

B. Urine for Bence Jones protein: Although urine for Bence Jones protein should certainly be performed in all suspected myelomas, it is extremely rare for light chain disease to cause clinically apparent hyperviscosity. This is because viscosity is directly proportional to the size of the molecule causing it therefore, IgM, which is pentameric, is most likely to cause hyperviscosity, followed by the dimeric IgA, then IgG.

A. Bone scan: Bone scanning is of value in multiple myeloma, but of no utility in Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia due to only very rare reports of skeletal system involvement.

D. Skeletal survey: The skeleton is usually not involved in Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia, meaning that a skeletal survey is not usually considered of value in the workup of the condition.

E. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain: MRI brain may show periventricular white matter changes, but it is not helpful in differentiating whether these are due to microvascular disease or due to an underlying hyperviscosity syndrome.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man is admitted to hospital with confusion. His wife says he has been complaining of abdominal pain and, in his confused state, suffered a head injury. He has a background of angina.

Examination is difficult, but unremarkable.

Observations:
Blood pressure 110/60 mmHg
Heart rate 120 bpm, regular

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)96 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.9 × 109/L4.0-11.0 × 109/L
Platelets (PLT)360 × 109/L150-400 × 109/L
Sodium (Na)135 mmol/L135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.6 mmol/L3.5-5.0 mmol/L
Urea12.2 mmol/L2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)132 μmol/L50-120 μmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca2+)3.6 mmol/L2.2-2.7 mmol

Electrocardiogram (ECG): Reduced QT interval
A CT head done in Accident and Emergency shows multiple lytic lesions.

What is the most important initial step?
questions.explanation:
D. Intravenous (IV) fluids: This patient has hypercalcaemia, most likely due to metastatic cancer or multiple myeloma. Patients are described as presenting with bone pain, renal stones, confusion and abdominal pain (bones, stones, psychic moans and abdominal groans). IV fluids can lead to a modest, but relatively rapid, fall in serum calcium, so this would be the first option here.

C. Prednisolone: Steroids do lower serum calcium, more modestly where there is an underlying solid neoplasm versus a haematological malignancy, but they take a number of hours to do this.

A. Bendroflumethiazide: Thiazide diuretics reduce calcium excretion and are therefore likely to further increase calcium levels in this situation.

B. Furosemide: Loop diuretics do reduce serum calcium, but in the presence of dehydration, their use is not advised, and IV fluids are the preferred initial intervention.

E. IV bisphosphonate: IV bisphosphonates are appropriate but take 1-2 days before their use is associated with a significant fall in serum calcium.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old man presents with tiredness of three months' duration. He has had abdominal pains in the past year that are fleeting in nature, and he has lost one stone in weight. He is on antacids and has no significant previous medical history.

On examination, he is slim with pale conjunctivae, but otherwise, there is nothing abnormal to find.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)55 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.3 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)523 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Ferritin5 μg/l20-250 μg/l
Corrected Calcium (Ca2+)2.05 mmol/l2.1-2.7 mmol/l

Colonoscopy and gastroscopy are normal (although gastroscopy was abandoned before biopsies were taken due to patient discomfort).

Which investigation would be most useful in making a diagnosis?
options: E. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine
questions.explanation:
D. Tissue transglutaminase antibodies: This gentleman's anaemia is due to iron deficiency, and the most likely cause is blood loss or iron malabsorption within the gastrointestinal tract. Repeating invasive imaging is unlikely to have as high a yield as tissue transglutamase antibodies, which may reveal an underlying diagnosis of coeliac disease, particularly as this patient failed to tolerate the gastroscopy well last time.

A. Repeat colonoscopy and gastroscopy: An adequately prepared colonoscopy and gastroscopy is likely to exclude significant pathology from the oesophagus, stomach and colon, and thus repeating them has limited utility versus other investigations.

B. Isotope-labelled red cell scan: Isotope-labelled red cell scans are useful to exclude significant bleeding, not the limited chronic blood loss which is likely here.

C. Isotope-labelled white cell scan: Isotope-labelled white cell scans are most useful in locating occult intra-abdominal abscesses.

E. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine: Given that there is evidence of iron deficiency anaemia, bone marrow examination is not of value in this case.

questions.question:
A 73-year-old woman who has long standing CLL comes to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath some 3 weeks after receiving a 3-unit blood transfusion for haemolytic anaemia. Her haemoglobin has fallen from 100g/l on discharge to 61g/l today. She has been treated with Fludarabine therapy for some months.

Which of the following is the primary pathogenic mechanism in Autoimmune Haemolytic anaemia, (AIHA) associated with CLL?
options: E. Pathological B cell antibody production
questions.explanation:
B. Autoreactive T cell induction: The answer is Autoreactive T cell induction - Autoreactive T cells specific for rhesus family antigens are commonly identified in patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. These in turn are thought to drive B cell antibody production, in tandem driving autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Most patients respond to corticosteroids, and in patients who fail to respond to corticosteroids, Rituximab can be considered for rescue therapy.

C. Autoreactive B cell induction: Autoreactive B cell induction is incorrect. B cells that produce antibodies to red cell components are upregulated in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia related to CLL although this is not the primary event.

A. Antigen presenting cell dysfunction: Antigen presenting cell dysfunction is incorrect, although it is known that CLL cells may display B3, a prominent component of the red cell membrane. Thus they act as antigen presenting cells themselves.

D. Monocyte dysfunction: Monocyte dysfunction, is incorrect because monocyte dysfunction is not a prominent feature of CLL.

E. Pathological B cell antibody production: Pathological B cell antibody production is incorrect. B cells that produce antibodies to red cell components are upregulated in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia related to CLL although this is not the primary event.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old African man, known to be homozygous for sickle cell disease, presents to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, right-sided pleuritic pain and dry cough over the last 12 hours. On examination, he has a fever of 38 °C. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations on air are 90%. He is tachycardic and normotensive, and chest examination demonstrates a widespread expiratory wheeze.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)60 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)20 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)450 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Chest X-rayNew shadowing at right base

He is diagnosed with acute chest syndrome, possibly related to Mycoplasma infection.

What further investigation should be completed to guide prognosis and management in this case?
options: C. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest
questions.explanation:
A. Arterial blood gas (ABG): The appearance of a new pulmonary infiltrate on the chest radiograph of a patient with sickle cell disease is termed 'acute chest syndrome'. The syndrome can develop because of infection or infarction, or a combination of the two. Infective causes include Gram-positive or -negative bacteria, atypical bacteria and viruses. Usual organisms include Pneumococcus, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia. Acute chest syndrome is usually accompanied or preceded by pain in the chest or extremities, fever, respiratory distress and/or low oxygen saturations. The white cell count is generally high. Although the chest radiograph may be normal initially, subsequent radiographs will reveal an infiltrate, which may extend rapidly, involving one or more lobes as well as the pleura.

Predictors of severity in acute chest syndrome include worsening hypoxia (< 10% reduction in pa(O2) from the patient's baseline or pa(O2) < 8 kPa), increasing respiratory rate, decreased PLT count, decreasing haemoglobin (Hb) concentration, multilobar involvement on chest X-ray and neurological complications.

Arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling is the gold standard in determining pa(O2) and pa(CO2) in patients with acute chest syndrome. It should be performed in all adults with peripheral oxygen saturations of < 94% on air. The ABG should be performed on room air (even if the patient is receiving oxygen) unless the patient is in respiratory distress or their peripheral oxygen saturations drop to below 85% after a few seconds on room air. The results of the ABG can guide prognosis (by severity) and further management with blood transfusion and respiratory support.

B. Hb electrophoresis: Haemoglobin (Hb) electrophoresis may be used to determine a patient's level of sickle cell haemoglobin (HbS). While this can be a helpful investigation over the long term, the level of HbS in patients with acute chest syndrome is not predictive of severity, nor will it aid in guiding further management.

C. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest: Although studies have shown that the extent of microvascular occlusion on HRCT correlates with the clinical severity and degree of hypoxia, it is not recommended in patients presenting with acute chest syndrome. This is because of the high dose of radiation delivered in HRCT and the fact that acute chest syndrome tends to recur and people with sickle cell disease frequently require other radiological tests. As it is not routinely recommended, it would not be appropriate for this patient.

D. Measurement of peak flow: Incentive spirometry is recommended in sickle cell patients presenting with chest or rib pain, as it has proven beneficial in preventing acute chest syndrome. It should also be considered alongside chest physiotherapy in patients presenting with acute chest syndrome. However, peak flow measurement is not of value in predicting the severity of acute chest syndrome or guiding management.

E. Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) lung scan: Although pulmonary embolism is a differential diagnosis in acute chest syndrome and ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) Q scanning may be considered to rule this out while reducing the radiation dose, research shows that V/Q scanning in patients with acute chest syndrome usually reveals widespread perfusion defects with normal ventilation, the appearances of which may be confused with pulmonary emboli when these are not actually present. It is not recommended as an initial investigation by the British Society for Haematology.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with indigestion of seven weeks' duration. She has no ongoing medical problems, and is otherwise asymptomatic. She is on no medication.

Examination is unremarkable. She undergoes gastro-oesophageal endoscopy, which reveals gastritis. Stomach biopsies confirm the presence of a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (maltoma/marginal zone lymphoma) of low-grade type; Helicobacter pylori is demonstrated. Computed tomography (CT) of chest, abdomen and pelvis reveals no additional disease, and a bone marrow trephine is unremarkable; the stomach wall is not clearly thickened.

What treatment would you recommend?
options: A. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP)
questions.explanation:
C. H. pylori eradication therapy: Maltomas, also known as marginal zone lymphomas, are low-grade lymphomas, most often diagnosed in the stomach. They are peculiar in that they are often associated with chronic inflammation of one of the following types:

  • In the stomach secondary to chronic H. pylori gastritis
  • In the eyes secondary to Sjogren syndrome
  • In the thyroid secondary to Hashimoto's thyroiditis
  • In the intestine secondary to Crohn's or coeliac disease.

Treatment against H. pylori is safe and will cause regression in 90% of low-grade gastric maltomas; response is less likely if cytogenetic abnormalities have been acquired (t11:18 being the most common), or if the muscularis mucosa has been invaded. This patient has early-stage disease, so triple therapy coupled with close oncological and gastroenterological follow-up is appropriate.

D. Partial gastrectomy: Surgery is rarely employed in the treatment of gastric maltoma, because it is usually not curative and results in significant operative morbidity.

A. Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP): R-CHOP (including rituximab) is a treatment option for more advanced gastric lymphoma.

B. Observation alone: Observation alone risks significant lymphoma progression, meaning that H. pylori eradication would then in all likelihood be ineffective.

E. High-dose dexamethasone: High-dose dexamethasone may provide symptomatic improvement, but is ineffective in treating H. pylori, the likely trigger for maltoma seen here.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of fever and lethargy. He had finished a third cycle of chemotherapy for osteosarcoma only a few days earlier and he has an indwelling central venous catheter.

On examination, he looks unwell. He has a fever of 38.9 °C and his BP is 90/60 mmHg, with a heart rate of 95 bpm and regular. There are no signs of pharyngitis and only minor erythema around the exit site for his catheter.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin104 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.4 × 109/l4-11 × 109/l
Neutrophils0.2 x 109/l2.5-7.58 x 109/l
Platelets125 x 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.3 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine122 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)174 IU/l5-30 IU/l
Alkaline phosphatase392 IU/l30-130 IU/l
Albumin26 g/l35-55 g/l

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
options: D. Piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin and fluconazole
questions.explanation:
B. Piperacillin/tazobactam: This patient has febrile neutropenia, having recently completed a course of chemotherapy, and has an indwelling vascular catheter. Hence a broad-spectrum antibacterial regimen, including adequate staphylococcal and pseudomonal cover, is recommended. Therapy is not delayed while awaiting sample results, and antifungal therapy is usually considered later if non-response to therapy is seen. The rise in alkaline phosphatase levels seen here may be due to hepatic dysfunction or related to the underlying bony tumour. Guidelines from the NICE recommend the use of monotherapy with piperacillin and tazobactam as the first line. Additional agents can be added later, depending on culture sensitivities and local protocols.

C. Piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin: The NICE guidelines recommend avoiding the use of aminoglycosides (such as gentamicin) as monotherapy or dual therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam for treatment of neutropenic sepsis, unless there are specific microbiological indications.

A. Gentamicin, vancomycin, flucloxacillin: Piperacillin/tazobactam is the cornerstone of therapy, according to the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. Therefore, the combination of gentamicin, vancomycin and flucloxacillin is inappropriate.

D. Piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin and fluconazole: Guidelines from the NICE recommend monotherapy with piperacillin/tazobactam for the treatment of neutropenic sepsis. Dual therapy with gentamicin is not recommended, unless microbiology dictates. In practice, antifungals are introduced in the event that a response to therapy is not seen at 48 hours, but not in the initial stages.

E. Piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin: Vancomycin is not indicated in the initial management of neutropenic sepsis, unless methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is suspected. Piperacillin/tazobactam is recommended as monotherapy initially.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman who was recently diagnosed to have Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (WM) presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of headache and blurring of vision. She has not been started on any medications for the disease previously.

The patient is willing to go through any treatment regimen as recommended by the doctor.

Which of the following is the best next step in the management of the patient?
options: E. Rituximab, bortezomib and dexamethasone (× 4-6 cycles)
questions.explanation:
C. Plasmapheresis: This patient's presentation is consistent with hyperviscosity syndrome. Further, fundoscopy has revealed evidence of branch retinal vein occlusion with retinal haemorrhage, which establishes the diagnosis of hyperviscosity syndrome. In such patients, emergency plasmapheresis is recommended as the first line of management. Once the symptoms have resolved, more definitive immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy is recommended.

B. Immediate treatment with ibrutinib: Ibrutinib is a bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor and is the first drug approved for use in relapsed or progressive WM. It is not beneficial in hyperviscosity syndrome.

A. Cladribine monotherapy (× 4 cycles): Cladribine is an alkylating agent that was previously widely used in the treatment of WM. However, it is not recommended for the treatment of hyperviscosity syndrome.

D. Rituximab monotherapy (× 4 cycles): In treatment-naïve patients with WM, initiation of rituximab would be a reasonable option when there is a low disease burden. However, this patient has presented with features of hyperviscosity syndrome and initiation of rituximab is not the best line of action in such patients.

E. Rituximab, bortezomib and dexamethasone (× 4-6 cycles): In treatment-naïve patients with WM, initiation of combination therapy with rituximab, bortezomib and dexamethasone would be a reasonable option when there is a high disease burden. However, this patient has presented with features of hyperviscosity syndrome and initiation of combination therapy with these drugs is not the best line of action in such patients.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with myelodysplasia complains of breathlessness on exertion. He was diagnosed with myelodysplasia three years ago and has since been on two units of blood every three weeks to maintain his haemoglobin (Hb) level above 100 g/l. He has noticed over the last three months increasing exertional breathlessness despite maintaining his haemoglobin level > 100.

Examination shows a slim man with greyish skin colour, with a heart rate of 90 bpm in sinus rhythm. Heart sounds are normal. The jugular venous pressure is not raised. The cardiac apex is palpable at the anterior axillary line. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest, and the abdominal examination is normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)113 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)1.3 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)23 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Neutrophils0.3 × 109/l2.5-7.58 × 109/l
Glucose12.4 mmol/l3.5-5.5 mmol/l

What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: A. Commence iron chelation with penicillamine
B. Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine
C. Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise Hb level to 120 g/l
D. Increase the transfusion programme to maintain Hb level above 120 g/l
E. Reduce the frequency of blood transfusions
questions.explanation:
B. Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine: This patient has early signs of iron overload secondary to chronic blood transfusion; grey skin, early heart failure and diabetes. There are limited options for intervention, and given the transfusion needs of this patient with iron overload, desferrioxamine is the most appropriate choice. It needs to be given for 8-12 hours per day for 5-7 days per week and is, therefore, a major undertaking for the patient. Side-effects of therapy are common and include high-frequency deafness and retinopathy.

A. Commence iron chelation with penicillamine: Penicillamine is a copper-chelating compound that removes copper from the body. It is used in the treatment of Wilson's disease where there is an excess of copper in the body. However, it does not have a role in chelating iron.

C. Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise Hb level to 120 g/l: Commencing erythropoietin to reduce the transfusion requirement is an attractive option. However, it is only likely to work in patients with low transfusion requirements (< 1 unit per month) and does not address the underlying problem of iron overload.

D. Increase the transfusion programme to maintain Hb level above 120 g/l: Increasing the transfusion programme runs the risk of further worsening iron overload and will not improve symptoms of cardiac failure.

E. Reduce the frequency of blood transfusions: The problem in this patient is due to secondary haemochromatosis. While reducing the frequency of transfusions might slow the progression of the disease, the patient might become anaemic and without chelation, there will be no reduction in the excessive iron levels in the patient.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man presents with worsening headaches, three TIAs in the past 6 months and exertional angina. He is a smoker of 30 cigarettes per day and has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily.

On examination, his BP is 165/90 mmHg and he looks plethoric.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)185 g/l135 - 175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)14.1 × 109/l4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)520 × 109/l150 - 400 × 109/l
Potassium (K+)5.4 mmol/l3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)160 μmol/l50 - 120 μmol/l

Which of the following results of further investigations is most likely to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythaemia?
options: A. Hypoxia on arterial blood gas testing
B. Hypercapnia on arterial blood gas testing
questions.explanation:
C. Low erythropoietin: Patients with primary polycythaemia carry a mutation that leads to hypersensitivity to erythropoietin. As such, even in the presence of low erythropoietin levels there is a drive to produce more red blood cells. The symptoms seen here are due to increased red cell mass, consequent increase in plasma volume and raised plasma viscosity.

An activating mutation in JAK2 is identified in many patients diagnosed with primary polycythaemia; this induces EPO hypersensitivity. Eventual transformation of primary polycythaemia may occur to acute myeloid leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or chronic myeloid leukaemia.

D. Elevated CO levels: These are elevated in carbon monoxide poisoning. Elevated CO levels of at least 3-4% in non-smokers and at least 10% in smokers are significant. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating an elevated level of carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO).

A. Hypoxia on arterial blood gas testing: Chronic hypoxia can cause secondary polycythaemia. This can be due to various conditions such as respiratory diseases (COPD, asthma) or cardiac causes (heart failure). It is not a marker used to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythaemia.

B. Hypercapnia on arterial blood gas testing: Hypercapnia is a marker of respiratory conditions such as COPD. Again, this will lead to secondary polycythaemia with raised erythropoietin levels.

E. Raised viscosity: This is not a specific test and can be raised in inflammatory, infectious and autoimmune conditions.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman presents to her General Practioner complaining of lethargy. Her past history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine and bendroflumethiazide; osteoarthritis for which she takes paracetamol; recurrent urinary tract infections for which she is currently taking a 6-week course of cephalexin; and epilepsy, for which she takes sodium valproate.

On examination, she looks pale and her skin is yellow-tinged. Her heart rate is 100 bpm and regular, and her BP is 110/70 mmHg. Direct Coomb's test is positive; serum haptoglobins are low; reticulocyte count is elevated. Urine dipstick is positive for blood. You suspect haemolysis.

Which of the following agents is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation:
C. Cephalexin: The more common causes of drug-induced autoimmune haemolytic anaemia include penicillin and penicillin derivatives, cephalosporins, levodopa, methyldopa, quinidine and some non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Discontinuing the causative agent usually leads to a rapid improvement in the condition, and a short course of oral prednisolone may accelerate recovery.

A. Paracetamol: The main concern with respect to use of paracetamol is hepatic failure rather than haemolytic anaemia. Given that this is a widely used over-the-counter medication, it has an excellent safety profile.

B. Sodium valproate: Sodium valproate can cause anaemia, but this is related to bone marrow abnormalities rather than to haemolytic anaemia. These bone marrow abnormalities resolve on discontinuation of the medication.

D. Amlodipine: Amlodipine in rare cases is associated with reductions in the white blood cell count and/or low platelets.

E. Bendroflumethiazide: Blood dyscrasias are rarely reported in patients treated with thiazides, although these are not related to haemolytic anaemia.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man is brought unconscious to the Emergency Department. He had been found at his sheltered accommodation by the warden, who brought in his medications: warfarin, furosemide and amoxicillin (10-day course, five days' doses used).

Examination shows a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 5/15, a dilated left-sided pupil and right-sided upper motor neurone signs in the upper and lower limbs. A computed tomography scan of the brain shows a large left-sided subdural haematoma. Ten milligrams of intravenous (IV) vitamin K are given immediately.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)5.3 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)403 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)43 seconds23.0-35.0 seconds
International normalised ratio (INR)2.0 (target INR 2.5)

What additional therapy should be administered to reverse this patient's warfarin?
options: A. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) up to 3000 U according to body weight
B. An additional dose of vitamin K 10 mg IV
E. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) 15 ml/kg stat
questions.explanation:
A. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) up to 3000 U according to body weight: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) contains vitamin K-dependent factors and normalises clotting within minutes of administration. It is the recommended product for life-threatening bleeding due to anticoagulation with warfarin. It is plasma-derived, so there is a potential risk of transfusion-transmitted infection, and it is prothrombotic. Even though the international normalised ratio (INR) is within the target range, it is still elevated, as compared to a patient not treated with warfarin, and therefore, it is reasonable to assume it has contributed towards the subdural haematoma and the patient's clinical state. It is therefore appropriate to rapidly reverse the INR with PCC.

B. An additional dose of vitamin K 10 mg IV: Vitamin K given intravenous (IV) will start to affect the INR for prothrombin activity within 4-8 hours. However, this patient is showing signs of temporal lobe herniation (ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil) and needs immediate cessation of bleeding if he is to survive.

C. Cryoprecipitate 10 U: Cryoprecipitate contains predominantly fibrinogen and factor VIII. It is, therefore, less effective in reversing bleeding due to warfarin, compared to PCC.

D. Factor VIII bypassing agent: Contained in Factor VIII bypassing agents are activated factors II, VII, IX and X, and it is highly thrombogenic. Its main use is in the management of acquired inhibitors in haemophilia.

E. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) 15 ml/kg stat: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains low levels of coagulation factors and it is estimated that even at a dose of 15 ml/kg, levels of most factors will only approach 20% of normal. In addition, the large volumes of FFP required are likely to precipitate pulmonary oedema, particularly in an elderly man on furosemide. It is only really considered if other options such as PCC are not available.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old Caucasian with a 4-month history of non-specific chest pain is seen in your Outpatient Clinic. She had been having intermittent twinges that initially settled with mild analgesics, but they have become more frequent and painful of late. She is most aware of them just underneath her sternum and there is no radiation. Movement does not exacerbate the pain. However, the more severe pains make her feel dizzy and she has almost passed out on three occasions. There is no history of night sweats, weight loss or fever. She is not short of breath on exertion, but admits that recently she has been too tired to play sport. She does not smoke or take illicit drugs and has recently gone off alcohol. She had asthma as a child but rarely used her salbutamol inhaler. She is on the oral contraceptive pill and has a steady boyfriend.

On examination, she looks tired and slightly anxious. She is afebrile. Her pulse is 64 bpm and regular, BP 105/62 mmHg, respirations at rest 16 breaths/min and saturations 97% on room air. She has a small lymph node in the left submandibular region. Heart sounds are normal, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft with no enlarged organs. ECG shows sinus rhythm. Chest X-ray PA reveals an enlarged mediastinum, with clear lung fields; an anterior mediastinal mass can be seen on the lateral chest X-ray.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)89 g/l115-155 g/l
White Cell Count (WCC)6.4 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)165 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Sodium (Na+)139 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)68 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
Urea4.1 mmol/l2.5-6.5 mmol/l
Glucose4.9 mmol/l3.5-5.5 mmol/l
Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)1652 IU/l100-190 IU/l
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)79.3 fl80-100 fl

CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass with irregular borders, 10.1 cm × 9.3 cm × 5.6 cm, surrounding the left pulmonary artery and ligamentum arteriosum; no infiltration of surrounding tissues; a large group of lymph nodes in the left axilla; no abnormalities in the abdomen and pelvis. Bone marrow biopsy shows non-specific fibrous tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Hodgkin's lymphoma: Hodgkin's lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes. Some 25% of patients have a constitutional upset (i.e. night sweats, weight loss, fever, pruritus and lethargy). Rarely, there may be alcohol-induced pain or features due to mass effects of the affected nodes. An isolated bone marrow biopsy may not yield any significant results as Hodgkin's disease can cause patchy bone marrow infiltration, Lymph node biopsies are often more useful. Reed-Sternberg cells are evident on microscopy. Treatment depends on classification and staging, but usually involves multiple chemotherapy agents. Prognosis is usually good.

B. Hairy cell leukaemia: Patients with hairy cell leukaemia have infiltration of the bone marrow by malignant B lymphocytes (the 'hairy cells'). This leads to failure to produce red blood cells, white bloods cells and platelets. Leukaemic cells accumulate within the spleen, leading to massive splenomegaly. Fatigue is also a key sign. Not all patients with hairy cell leukaemia require treatment but, if they do, often single-agent treatment will suffice. This patient's presentation is not in keeping with a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.

C. Malignant teratoma: A differential for an anterior mediastinal mass includes teratoma. However, teratomas are extremely rare and are often associated with pelvic disease, which the patient in this case does not have. These are usually tumours that develop in utero but that are only picked up much later on in life. Diagnosis is usually via histology. Some teratomas contain yolk sac elements that secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). However, AFP levels are more commonly used to monitor for disease recurrence after diagnosis rather than being diagnostic.

D. Thymoma: This patient has an anterior mediastinal mass which could be in keeping with a thymoma. However, the mass in this patient has irregular borders and usually with a thymoma you see a smooth, encapsulated tumour.

E. Tuberculosis: This patient has a clear lung fields on CT where you would normally expect to find lesions. The patient also is not suffering with temperatures, productive cough or haemoptysis, all of which make a diagnosis of TB less likely.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward with an 8-day history of fevers, vomiting and diarrhoea. He has been unable to tolerate oral intake and reports feeling lethargic. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin and gliclazide.

During his admission, he spikes a fever of 39.5 °C with a heart rate of 128 bpm and regular with a BP of 90/60mmHg. Auscultation of his chest is clear, with oxygen saturations of 94% on air. His abdomen is soft with generalised discomfort. There is significant bruising around the BP cuff site.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultsNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)115 g/l115-155 g/l
White cell count (WCC)18.7 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)20 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Sodium (Na+)138 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.9 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Urea15.1 mmol/l1.8-7.1 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)280 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
C-reactive protein (CRP)144 mg/l< 10 mg/l
Activated partial prothrombin time50 s27-41 s
Prothrombin time18 s12-15 s
Fibrinogen1.2 g/l1.9-8.0 g/l
Blood cultureGram-negative rods, awaiting full culture report

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation: This patient has a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), likely secondary to Gram-negative septic shock. DIC is an acquired syndrome characterised by dysregulation of the coagulation system leading to the formation of thrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors that, in turn, leads to bleeding. Laboratory markers of DIC include a prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial prothrombin time and decreased fibrinogen and platelet count. Another laboratory marker is the presence of elevated fibrin degradation products (D-dimer).

B. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The syndrome presents with a history of gastrointestinal upset and is most commonly caused by Shiga-like toxin-producing Escherichia coli (0157:H7). This patient has two of these characteristics and evidence of Gram-negative rods in the bloodstream that may be suggestive of Escherichia coli. However, this patient does not have anaemia and the acute kidney injury could also be caused by eight days of dehydration secondary to diarrhoea, vomiting and reduced oral intake. A good distinguishing factor between HUS and DIC is the prothrombin time which is usually normal in patients with HUS. A prolonged prothrombin time is suggestive of DIC.

C. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is a severe drug reaction to heparin that is characterised by the activation of platelets to produce a hypercoagulable state. The onset of HIT tends to follow 5-10 days of exposure to heparin, including unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin or fondaparinux. Coagulation studies may be normal or abnormal in HIT, as HIT can also induce DIC. However, this patient is not displaying features of thrombosis; rather, he is showing signs of bleeding with significant bruising, making HIT unlikely.

D. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is a haematological disorder characterised by isolated thrombocytopenia. Sometimes thrombocytopenia may be idiopathic or follow a preceding viral illness. Although this patient has marked thrombocytopenia, the presence of other coagulopathic features makes DIC the much more likely diagnosis.

E. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is characterised by a pentad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute renal impairment, cerebral dysfunction and fever. Causes of TTP range from being idiopathic or secondary to infection or pregnancy. Typically, patients will expect to have anaemia and thrombocytopenia, but a deranged coagulation profile is not a feature of TTP.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man presents to the clinic with fever, weight loss, lethargy and a sensation of pins and needles in his feet. He is particularly concerned that he has begun to suffer increasing headaches over the past few weeks.

Other past history of note is gout, which developed a few months ago. On examination, there are lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/l (normal MCV)135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.1 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)95 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Sodium (Na+)141 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)5.1 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)145 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)75 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Immunoglobulin M (IgM)Paraprotein band
Bone marrowPlasma cell infiltration

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (WM): The combination of anaemia with low white cell and platelet counts, raised ESR, plasma cell infiltration of bone marrow and IgM paraprotein band is highly suggestive of Waldenström's. Death occurs either due to cardiovascular events because of increased viscosity, or due to progression of bone marrow infiltration leading to suppressed response to infection. Frontline chemotherapy for Waldenström's includes the use of alkylating agents; for patients who suffer from acute manifestations of hyperviscosity syndrome, plasmapheresis is the treatment of choice.

A. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): CLL is associated with splenomegaly, although the predominant abnormality seen is a rise in peripheral blood white count.

C. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL): ALL is usually associated with severe anaemia and thrombocytopenia, with recurrent infections and bleeding episodes, rather than the picture seen here.

D. Myelofibrosis: Myelofibrosis is not associated with symptoms of hyperviscosity (the neuropathy and headaches seen here).

E. Myelodysplasia: Like myelofibrosis, myelodysplasia is not associated with the hyperviscosity symptoms reported here.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department with severe back pain that came on while he was ice-skating. He has recently recovered from a viral upper respiratory tract infection, but is otherwise fit and well. He developed back pain without any obvious trauma, and passed dark red urine: he has not passed urine since (four hours ago). He is on no medications and does not smoke or drink. There is no family history of note.

On examination, he is in severe discomfort, temperature 38.3 °C, pulse 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 145/83 mmHg, peripheries are well perfused and there is no cyanosis. He is icteric. Abdominal, respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)83 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)4.7 × 109/l4.0-11.0 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)263 × 109/l150-400 × 109/l
Reticulocytes145 × 109/l25-100 × 109/l
Blood filmMacrophages with ingested erythrocytes
Creatinine (Cr)195 μmol/l50-120 μmol/l
Direct Coomb's test at room temperatureNegative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria: This patient has developed acute intravascular haemolysis (anaemia, high reticulocyte count, jaundice, haemoglobinuria) in response to cold exposure. In PCH, an antibody that binds temporarily in the cold develops in response to infection - classically syphilis, but more commonly various viral infections including Epstein-Barr virus - and on warming, dissociates and activates complement, causing rapid intravascular haemolysis, with rigors and severe bone pain. The antibody is to the P blood group, and is confirmed by the finding of a Donath-Landsteiner antibody - the patient's serum is incubated with red blood cells at 4°C and warmed, with subsequent haemolysis. P-negative blood (pp) can be used as a negative control. The Coombs test, now more appropriately called the direct agglutination test, is usually negative. Kidney disease can ensue, but patients in general have a single episode that responds to supportive care.

A. Cold haemagglutinin disease: Cold haemagglutinin disease is not usually paroxysmal in nature, and the Coombs test is positive for C3d: the blood film usually shows agglutination of red cells. Taking these factors together, cold haemagglutinin disease is incorrect.

C. Rhabdomyolysis: Rhabdomyolysis is associated with significant muscle necrosis and also with trauma, although none has been described here.

D. Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria: PNH is associated with repeated complement-mediated haemolysis and presents with more marked urinary discoloration in the morning.

E. Evan's syndrome: Evans is Coombs-positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, a rare condition of unknown aetiology.

questions.question:
A 71-year-old woman presents with tiredness and lethargy. Her GP had previously noted that she was anaemic and commenced iron therapy.

Abdominal examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal Values
White cell count (WCC)2.1 × 109 mmol/l4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l
Neutrophils0.9 × 109 mmol/l1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l
Lymphocytes0.8 × 109 mmol/l1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l
Monocytes0.1 × 109 mmol/l0 - 0.8 × 109/l
Eosinophils0 × 109 mmol/l0.04 - 0.4 × 109/l
Basophils0 × 109 mmol/l< 0.1 × 109/l
Haemoglobin (Hb)91 g/l135 - 175 g/l
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)102 fl80 - 100 fl
Platelets (PLT)90 × 109 mmol/l150 - 400 × 109/l

Bone marrow biopsy reveals increased cellularity with 10% ring sideroblast and <5% blast cells.

What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
C. Myelodysplasia: Myelodysplasia occurs mainly in the elderly and presents with anaemia, infection or bleeding due to pancytopenia. Serial blood counts show evidence of increasing bone marrow failure and the bone marrow shows increased cellularity.
